questions.title: Dividing responsibilities between enterprise apps and API development
questions.prompt: Serim Insurance, a multinational insurer, has deployed Claude Enterprise to all 8,000 employees for general work such as drafting and summarization. Its legal division is preparing automated reinsurance-contract review. Agreements with reinsurers require that **the provider not store prompts or responses after returning the response**. Contracts span hundreds of pages, making repeated transmission costs a concern, but the platform team must meet the requirement **without changing ordinary employees' existing experience**. Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep general work in Claude Enterprise and build contract review in a separate ZDR-enabled Claude API organization. Upload the long contracts once to the Files API and reference `file_id` rather than retransmitting them on every request.
Reduce the existing Claude Enterprise organization's custom retention period to the shortest permitted value and conduct contract reviews only in chats outside projects.

Keep general work in Claude Enterprise and build contract review using the Messages API in a separate ZDR-enabled Claude API organization. Include contract text directly in every request and accept the transmission cost.
Move all company usage to a custom Claude API chat application and handle general work and contract review together in one ZDR organization for a unified retention policy.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are no storage after the response and preserving ordinary employees' existing experience. Anthropic's documentation states that ZDR is enabled per organization and applies to eligible Claude API features such as Messages; Claude Team and Enterprise interfaces are not eligible. Features such as the Files API, Batch, and code execution are not blocked in ZDR organizations, but their feature-specific retention policies apply to data when used. Therefore, route only the no-storage workload through the ZDR organization's Messages API and accept repeated transmission costs.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Separation into a ZDR API organization is appropriate and reduces cost, but the Files API is ineligible for ZDR and retains files until deletion or expiration, so contracts remain stored after responses.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; appropriate for a different situation)**: The minimum custom retention period is 30 days. Deletion after a defined period is different from no storage after a response.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Only the affected workload uses a genuinely ZDR-eligible path, preserving ordinary employees' environment. Retransmitting contracts is the tradeoff.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; overengineered)**: One policy is simpler, but rebuilding company-wide chat for a requirement affecting only one workload adds operational burden and violates the existing-experience constraint.

Additional note: The account team enables ZDR separately for each organization; it does not automatically extend to other organizations under the same account.

**References**: [API and data retention › Zero data retention (ZDR)](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/api-and-data-retention) · [Configure custom data retention controls for Enterprise plans](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/10440198-configure-custom-data-retention-controls-for-enterprise-plans)

questions.title: Selecting provider delivery paths for present and future requirements
questions.prompt:
Global manufacturer Daewon Tech runs two Claude API workloads: an engineering agent uses the MCP connector to call internal remote MCP tools, and quality-report summaries run nightly through Message Batches. A German factory's quality-analysis assistant will launch in 2027. Requirements:

- The German assistant needs a current model at Claude Sonnet 5.5 capability and **EU-only inference**.
- The group has a large Google Cloud commitment, which the CFO wants to use as much as possible.
- **Do not migrate if existing functionality would be lost**.

Select **2** decisions meeting current and future requirements.

options.text: Move headquarters' overnight summarization to Claude on Google Cloud to use the commitment, retaining existing Message Batches code with only endpoint and authentication changes.
Call Claude on Google Cloud through the `eu` multi-region endpoint for the German assistant and include the endpoint's 10% premium in the budget.
Keep the German assistant on the Claude API and enforce EU inference through `allowed_inference_geos` and `default_inference_geo` in a dedicated workspace.
Keep headquarters' MCP-connector engineering agent on the Claude API and apply the commitment to workloads that do not use the MCP connector, Batch, or Files API.
Consolidate every workload, including the headquarters agent, on Google Cloud's `global` endpoint to maximize commitment usage.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are EU-only inference and preserving currently used functionality. The Claude API's `inference_geo` supports only `global` and `us`, so it cannot meet EU inference requirements. Claude on Google Cloud determines geography through endpoints; the `eu` multi-region endpoint dynamically routes within the EU, and multi-region and regional endpoints carry a 10% premium. However, Google Cloud does not support features including the MCP connector, Message Batches, and Files API. Keep workloads dependent on them on the Claude API to use the spending commitment without losing features.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: Claude on Google Cloud does not support the Message Batches endpoint, so existing batch code cannot be reused unchanged. It uses the commitment but violates feature preservation.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: The multi-region endpoint satisfies EU inference and budgets for the premium. Bedrock and Google Cloud have their own retirement schedules, which must also be tracked separately by access route.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: `default_inference_geo` and `allowed_inference_geos` also accept only `global` and `us`; workspace geo, the storage location, currently supports only `us`.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: The MCP connector is available on the Claude API, Claude Platform on AWS, and Microsoft Foundry, while Google Cloud is not listed. Keep workloads needing it on the Claude API and use the commitment for workloads without those feature constraints.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: The `global` endpoint routes across regions according to capacity, failing strict residency requirements and losing the MCP connector and Batch.

Additional note: Single-region endpoints support strict single-region residency or Provisioned Throughput, but model availability varies by region. Check Model Garden for current-model support first.

**References**: [Claude on Google Cloud › Global, multi-region, and regional endpoints](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-on-vertex-ai) · [Claude on Google Cloud › Features not supported](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-on-vertex-ai) · [Data residency › Inference geo](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency) · [MCP connector › Compatibility](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector) · [Model deprecations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations)

questions.title: Assigning departmental needs to enterprise apps and API processing tiers
questions.prompt:
Nuri Retail has ChatGPT Enterprise for all employees and a ZDR-approved OpenAI API organization with project-level data controls. Company policy requires **workloads sending customer personal data to use only ZDR-eligible endpoints in ZDR projects**. Among configurations meeting requirements, choose **lowest operational burden first**, then **lowest cost**.

1. Sales: Personal productivity, including proposal drafts and meeting summaries. No customer personal data and no developers.
2. Data: Nightly sentiment classification of hundreds of thousands of reviews containing author names/contact details. Results are needed by the following morning; developers are available.
3. Support: Customer-facing chatbot exchanging personal data. Traffic is steady all day and response latency must be **consistently low**.

Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: 1 ChatGPT Enterprise / 2 Responses API with `service_tier: "flex"` in a ZDR project, retrying 429 with backoff / 3 Priority Responses API in a ZDR project
1 ChatGPT Enterprise / 2 Batch API in a ZDR project, bundling daily requests into one file for 50% savings / 3 Priority Responses API in a ZDR project
1 ChatGPT Enterprise / 2 Flex Responses API in a ZDR project, retrying 429 with backoff / 3 default Standard Responses API in a ZDR project
1 a custom internal OpenAI API chat app in a non-ZDR project / 2 Flex Responses API in a ZDR project with 429 retries / 3 Priority Responses API in a ZDR project

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are ZDR-eligible endpoints only, consistently low latency, and the operational-burden-then-cost priority. `/v1/responses` is ZDR-eligible with restrictions; `/v1/batches` and input-file endpoint `/v1/files` are not and retain data until deletion. Thus Batch, the usual bulk asynchronous solution, is prohibited here. Flex on a ZDR-eligible endpoint uses Batch rates and meets cost requirements. The tradeoff is slow responses and resource-unavailable 429s requiring retry logic, acceptable for the staffed Data team and next-morning deadline.

| Department | Decision rationale |
| --- | --- |
| 1 Sales | With no personal data or developers, the deployed enterprise app has the lowest operational burden. {{option:D}}'s custom chat adds development and operations. |
| 2 Data | Batch ({{option:B}}) offers 50% savings and a suitable 24-hour window but violates ZDR endpoint policy. Flex uses Batch rates; resource-unavailable 429s are unbilled, and exponential backoff suits latency-tolerant work. |
| 3 Support | Priority offers much lower and more consistent latency than Standard for steady user-facing traffic. Standard ({{option:C}}) is cheaper but cannot guarantee the required consistently low latency. Priority's tradeoff is a higher rate. |

Additional note: Flex is beta and supports limited models; verify the classification model on the pricing page. Projects can inherit organizational controls or individually select ZDR, Modified Abuse Monitoring, or None.

**References**: [Data controls in the OpenAI platform › Zero Data Retention](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) · [Flex processing › Resource unavailable errors](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/flex-processing) · [Priority processing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/priority-processing) · [Batch API › Overview](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch)

questions.title: Centrally controlling agents’ external tool calls
questions.prompt:
Hangyeol Energy deploys business-unit agents to Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform Agent Runtime. They call internal/external MCP servers and external APIs. Security requires:

- Connections **only to approved destinations**.
- Inspection of tool responses for prompt injection.
- **Central enforcement**, without adding control logic to every business-unit agent.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Deploy Agent Gateway in Client-to-Agent (ingress) mode with Model Armor to centrally inspect incoming client prompts.
Deploy Agent Gateway in Agent-to-Anywhere (egress) mode, register destinations in Agent Registry, and apply Model Armor inspection.
Have each business-unit agent call Model Armor directly for tool-response inspection and distribute destination allowlists through shared configuration.
Consolidate agents into one project and use VPC firewall rules to allow only approved external MCP/API IP addresses.

questions.explanation:
Agent Gateway is a network entry/exit point for agent interactions. Agent-to-Anywhere egress protects outbound calls to MCP servers, tools, and APIs. Egress processing checks IAM, Agent Registry, inspectors such as Model Armor, then forwards. Unregistered destinations require explicit URL IAM policies. This centrally enforces destination approval and response inspection without code changes.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; appropriate to another situation)**: Ingress protects client-to-agent access, such as Cursor or Claude Code. It does not control outbound destinations.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Egress combines Registry-based destination controls with Model Armor inspection.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: It works but embeds controls in every unit's code, violating centralized enforcement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; related-feature confusion)**: Network allowlists can block destinations but cannot inspect response content for injection; consolidation also weakens unit separation.

Additional note: Ingress gateways support either Model Armor or Semantic Governance policies, not both simultaneously.

**References**: [Agent Gateway overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/gateways/agent-gateway-overview) · [Model Armor overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/model-armor/overview)

questions.title: Promptly reflecting permission changes in shared retrieval
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Financial operates enterprise search by ingesting Confluence Cloud and Jira Cloud into Gemini Enterprise. Audit requires:

- Group membership changes reflected in search access permissions **within one hour**.
- Source-deleted documents removed from results **within one day**.

Which synchronization schedule is most appropriate?

options.text: Run full entity sync daily and incremental sync every three hours, relying on full entity sync for identity updates.
Run combined full identity/entity synchronization every three hours, the shortest configurable interval.
Run independent full identity sync every 30 minutes and only incremental entity sync every three hours.
Run independent full identity sync every 30 minutes, full entity sync daily, and incremental sync more frequently than full sync.

questions.explanation:
In Gemini Enterprise, identity sync maps users to ACL groups; full entity sync maps documents to groups and reflects deletions. Incremental sync imports only additions/updates, not identity changes or deletions. Independent full identity sync supports a 30-minute minimum, and full entity sync intervals range from three hours to seven days, so use separate types for the two requirements.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Daily full entity sync handles deletions, but identity sync handles user/group relationships and incremental sync excludes identity data, missing the one-hour deadline.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Deletions meet the deadline, but combined full sync's three-hour minimum misses one-hour permission updates.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Permissions meet the deadline, but incremental sync never reflects deletions.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Thirty-minute identity sync and daily full entity sync meet the respective deadlines. The tradeoff is managing three sync types.

Additional note: Incremental sync must run more frequently than full sync; equal intervals pause incremental sync, requiring manual resumption.

**References**: [Introduction to connectors and data stores › Data sync types and schedules](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/introduction-to-connectors-and-data-stores)

questions.title: Designing an internal tool layer shared across AI interfaces
questions.prompt:
Mirae Trading wants internal HR/ERP access from three interfaces: employees in ChatGPT Enterprise, automation agents in a ZDR Claude API organization, and another provider's agents planned for next year. Architecture principles:

- **Implement integration logic and authorization once** for current and future interfaces.
- Responses contain **only data each user can access in the source system**.
- Claude workloads **remain within ZDR coverage**.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Build remote MCP servers per system with per-user authentication. Add them as ChatGPT custom apps and call the same servers through Claude Messages MCP connector (`mcp_servers`) with per-user OAuth tokens.
Build remote MCP servers. Add them as admin-managed workspace connections using a shared service account in ChatGPT; have the Claude backend use client-side SDK MCP helpers with that same account.
Add per-user-authenticated MCP servers as ChatGPT custom apps, but separately implement Claude backend function tools wrapping HR/ERP REST APIs with user tokens.

Build per-user-authenticated remote MCP servers. An admin with custom-app permission adds them to ChatGPT; the Claude backend uses client-side SDK MCP helpers to call the same servers and expose them as ordinary tools.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are implement once, source-user permissions, and ZDR. ChatGPT Enterprise owners/admins or authorized members can add custom MCP apps. Apps requiring per-user authentication let each user connect their own account, preserving source permissions. Claude's MCP connector is not ZDR-eligible; exchanged server data follows standard retention. ZDR organizations can instead connect directly using client-side SDK MCP helpers and pass ordinary tools to Messages.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Reuse and user permissions are met, but MCP connector data leaves ZDR coverage.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Reuse and ZDR are met, but a shared service account does not enforce each user's source permissions in responses.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: Permissions and ZDR are met, but integration is duplicated per interface and must be rebuilt again for the next provider.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: All interfaces reuse one MCP server, per-user authentication propagates source permissions, and Claude uses only ZDR-eligible paths.

Additional note: OpenAI does not verify custom apps, so limit app-addition permission to a small group such as the platform team.

**References**: [Admin controls, security, and compliance in connectors › Custom apps](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11509118-admin-controls-security-and-compliance-in-connectors-enterprise-edu-and-business) · [MCP connector › Data retention](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector) · [MCP connector › Client-side MCP helpers](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector) · [API and data retention › Feature eligibility](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/api-and-data-retention)

questions.title: Isolating business-unit documents at the retrieval layer
questions.prompt:
Daehan Holdings wants one Gemini Enterprise environment to provide internal search for its pharmaceutical, chemical, and construction divisions. Each division operates its own SharePoint and Jira Cloud. Legal, security, and IT operations require:

- One division's **documents and search queries must not be transmitted or exposed to another division's systems**.
- Division data **must not share a data store**, because a divested division must be separable and deletable at data-store level.
- Even within a division, users must see **only documents they can access in the source SharePoint or Jira system**, without staff maintaining a duplicate permissions table.
- IT wants all three divisions in **one Gemini Enterprise environment, with one project and billing unit**.

Select TWO design decisions meeting all requirements.

options.text: Create one app, or engine, per division and connect each app only to data stores ingesting that division's sources.
Connect all three divisions' third-party sources to one app through federation and delegate authorization to source systems.
Configure access control for each source connection and use identity synchronization to map users and ACL groups so source permissions are reflected in results.
Create a separate Gemini Enterprise environment in a separate Google Cloud project for each division and connect only that division's sources.
Ingest documents from all three divisions into one data store, configuring identity synchronization and access control to hide results from users lacking source permissions.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are preventing cross-division document and query exposure, avoiding shared data stores, and retaining one environment. In Gemini Enterprise, apps connect to one or more data stores, and the relationship is many-to-many. Within one environment, connecting each division's app only to its own data stores separates both search scope and data boundaries. Source-specific access control and identity synchronization then preserve source permissions within each division.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: App connections separate search scope, division-specific data stores provide separation and deletion units, and one environment is retained.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It preserves source permissions and a single environment, but federation sends queries to all enabled third-party search backends, transmitting one division's queries to another's systems.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Identity synchronization maps users to ACL groups, and full synchronization maps documents to groups, reflecting source permissions without a separate permissions table.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Isolation and data boundaries are preserved, but separate environments violate the one-project, one-billing-unit constraint and triple administrative burden.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It preserves source permissions and one environment, but mixing divisions in one data store prevents division-level separation and deletion.

**References**: [Gemini Enterprise concepts](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/concepts) · [Introduction to connectors and data stores](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/introduction-to-connectors-and-data-stores)

questions.title: Combining Gemini API processing tiers by workload
questions.prompt:
Haneul Air uses Gemini 3.8 Flash for three workloads in one Gemini API project. **Only one project** is allowed to simplify billing and key management.

1. Booking chatbot: customer-facing; during weather-related spikes it must **take precedence over other traffic**. Some peak requests may fall back to Standard, but **must not fail with errors**.
2. Delay-notification agent: a three-step **synchronous chain**, each output feeding the next input. It must finish **within two hours**, ideally at half standard pricing.
3. Overnight regression evaluation: grade 50,000 prompts by the following evening at half standard pricing, **without consuming the chatbot's interactive request limits**.

Which combination is most appropriate?

options.text: 1 Priority, monitoring downgrade frequency in response headers / 2 submit chain stages sequentially as Batch jobs / 3 Batch API
1 Standard with exponential backoff / 2 Flex with retries, then explicit Standard retry if still failing / 3 Batch API
1 Priority, monitoring response-header downgrades / 2 Flex with retries, then explicit Standard retry if still failing / 3 Batch API
1 Priority with downgrade monitoring / 2 Flex with retries and explicit Standard fallback / 3 Flex using a dedicated evaluation API key

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are precedence without errors, a synchronous chain within two hours, and separate interactive limits within one project. Gemini Priority is a non-sheddable tier processed before Standard/Flex; requests exceeding dynamic Priority limits downgrade to Standard instead of erroring. Flex and Batch both offer 50% discounts. Flex is synchronous with minute-scale latency targets of 1–15 minutes, fitting dependent chains. Batch is asynchronous with an up-to-24-hour target and separate interactive limits. The correct solution pays Priority rates 75–100% above Standard for the chatbot.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; appropriate to another situation)**: Cost and limit isolation work, but each chain stage could take up to 24 hours in Batch, missing two hours.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Chatbot cost is lowest, but Standard does not take precedence over other traffic.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Priority's downgrade behavior preserves priority handling without errors; Flex provides half-price synchronous chaining; Batch isolates evaluation limits.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Costs and chain timing fit, but Gemini rate limits are project-scoped, not key-scoped, and Flex counts against normal limits. Separate keys still consume chatbot capacity, while separate projects are prohibited.

Additional note: Flex can be preempted by Standard traffic. To prevent unexpected charges, it never automatically upgrades to Standard; clients must implement retries/fallback. Inspect `x-gemini-service-tier` for Priority downgrades.

**References**: [Optimization › Tier comparison](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/optimization) · [Priority inference](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/priority-inference) · [Flex inference](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/flex-inference) · [Batch API](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/batch-mode) · [Rate limits](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits)

questions.title: Expanding Priority traffic while running evaluations
questions.prompt:
Fintech Baro Pay runs payment support in an OpenAI project whose default service tier is Priority, using one model at about 1.2M TPM. A new market launch next Monday will roughly double support traffic. Quality assurance runs tens of thousands of evaluations on the same model every Monday morning through Standard synchronous calls, increasing support 429s. Requirements:

- Maintain **Priority processing** on launch day. Rollout may be staged throughout the day as long as it finishes **that day**.
- Evaluations must **cost less** and **not compete for the same rate limits** as support. Results are needed within two days.

Select **2** actions.

options.text: Move evaluations to Batch for 50% savings, separate model limits, and a 24-hour completion window.
Switch evaluations to `service_tier: "flex"` at Batch rates, retrying resource-unavailable 429s with `auto` for standard processing.
Switch all new-market traffic at launch time and omit explicit `service_tier` because the project defaults to Priority.
Use feature flags to open new-market traffic over several hours and monitor responses reporting `service_tier: "default"`.
Use Standard for support on launch day to avoid ramp limits, then restore the project to Priority after traffic stabilizes.

questions.explanation:
The decisive cues are approximately 1.2M TPM, doubling, rollout allowed throughout the day, and no shared-limit competition. OpenAI Priority has a ramp limit: at 1M TPM or above, increasing TPM more than 50% within 15 minutes can downgrade some requests to Standard billing/processing. Documentation recommends shifting traffic over hours with feature flags. Priority and Standard share a model's limits, so synchronous evaluations continue competing. Batch limits are separate, resolving cost and contention together.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: A 50% discount, separate limits, and a 24-hour window satisfy lower cost, no contention, and the two-day deadline. Results are not immediate.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Rates decrease, but Standard retries after 429 still use model limits shared with support. Documented separate limits are provided by Batch.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Doubling 1.2M TPM at once triggers ramp conditions, risking Standard downgrades and violating continued Priority.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Same-day flexibility permits gradual ramping; downgraded responses report `service_tier="default"`.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: It avoids ramp limits by directly violating Priority-on-launch-day requirements. Changing the project tier back also migrates existing traffic gradually over time.

Additional note: Priority guidance discourages spiky evaluation/data-processing traffic and large ETL/batch jobs.

**References**: [Priority processing › Ramp rate limits](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/priority-processing) · [Batch API › Rate limits](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch) · [Flex processing › Resource unavailable errors](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/flex-processing)

questions.title: Combining shared-assistant cache efficiency with business-unit attribution
questions.prompt:
Seum Group has six business-unit workspaces in one Claude API organization. Each calls a shared internal-policy assistant from its own workspace. All use Claude Sonnet 5.5 with an identical 80,000-token policy prefix and prompt caching, but cache-read rates are much lower than expected. Requirements:

- Substantially reduce shared-prefix costs.
- Attribute usage by unit **in Console** for cost allocation.
- Use **provider-enforced limits** so assistant spikes do not block each unit's other work.
- **No new platform or organization**.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Create a dedicated assistant workspace, consolidate all calls there, attribute usage with per-unit API keys in Console, and configure workspace spend/rate limits.
Keep workspaces and keys unchanged but extend TTL to one hour to reduce expiry between calls.
Move the assistant to Claude on Google Cloud, whose organization-level cache isolation allows shared caching across separated callers.
Consolidate calls in Default Workspace and issue separate Default API keys per unit for Console export attribution.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are Console attribution, provider-side limits, and no new platform/organization. Claude API caches are workspace-isolated, so identical prefixes are written separately in six workspaces. Consolidating calls shares the cache; Console exports break down usage by API key/model, preserving unit attribution with separate keys. Workspace spending/rate caps protect other workloads from assistant spikes.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Shared caching, key-level attribution, and workspace caps all fit inside one organization.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; appropriate to another situation)**: TTL addresses expiry within a workspace, not cross-workspace isolation. Six writes remain, and one-hour writes cost twice base input, potentially increasing cost.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Bedrock/Google Cloud use organization-level cache isolation, enabling sharing, but moving platforms is prohibited.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Sharing and attribution work, but Default Workspace cannot have limits configured, leaving other work unprotected.

Additional note: Cache-read tokens do not count toward ITPM for most models, so consolidation improves rate-limit utilization as well as cost.

**References**: [Prompt caching › Cache storage and sharing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Rate limits › Setting lower limits for Workspaces](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits) · [Model deprecations › Auditing model usage](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations)

questions.title: Attributing business-unit usage across multiple providers
questions.prompt:
Hannuri Bio, a multinational pharmaceutical company, uses both the OpenAI API and Claude API and must charge AI costs back to twelve cost centers across five divisions. The CFO requires:

- **Cost-center usage** must be distinguishable in provider consoles.
- Providers must **enforce limits at division level** so one division's excessive use does not block another.
- Cost centers within a division **share the division limit**, without separate center-level partitions.
- Keep **only one organization per provider** to simplify operations.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep one API key per provider in a company-wide gateway and allocate usage using cost-center tags in gateway logs.
Create an OpenAI project and Claude workspace for each of the twelve cost centers, set limits for each project/workspace, and attribute costs using console usage.
Create a separate OpenAI organization and Claude organization for each division, issue cost-center API keys within each, and allocate costs using invoices and per-key usage.
Set custom rate and spending limits on division-specific OpenAI projects and Claude workspaces, issue dedicated API keys per cost center, and attribute costs using console usage.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are division-level enforcement, sharing limits within each division, one organization per provider, and console-visible cost-center usage. OpenAI supports custom project rate and spending limits and API-key usage on the Usage page. Claude supports workspace spending and rate limits, identifies the aggregation workspace through the `anthropic-workspace-id` response header, and exports usage by API key and model from Console Usage. Use projects/workspaces for division limits and keys beneath them for attribution. The tradeoff is no provider-enforced cost-center limits: one center can consume its division's allocation first, requiring alerts and internal adjustments afterward.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Gateway logs support allocation, but provider consoles cannot distinguish centers and provider-side division limits are absent.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Console attribution and provider enforcement work, but separate center-level limit units prevent sharing the division limit and complicate operations with twelve projects/workspaces.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Attribution and enforcement work, but multiplying organizations repeats retention policies such as ZDR, billing, and key management, violating one organization per provider.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Provider subunits enforce division limits, keys attribute cost-center usage, and each provider retains one organization.

**References**: [Production best practices](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/production-best-practices) · [Rate limits › How do these rate limits work?](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/rate-limits) · [Rate limits](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits) · [Model deprecations](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/model-deprecations)

questions.title: Enabling a retention-required model for one team in a ZDR organization
questions.prompt:
Justice Law's Claude API organization has ZDR and three workspaces:

- Default Workspace: a few administrator test keys, no production traffic.
- `cases`: production keys for client case-advice services.
- `dev-shared`: shared by R&D experiments and document-pipeline validation using real case documents.

R&D receives "organization or workspace must have data retention enabled" when calling Claude Fable 5.1 with a `dev-shared` key. Requirements:

- **Every call carrying client case data retains ZDR**.

Global media group Starlight Media runs generative AI applications across Google Cloud and other clouds. Security requires:

- **Enforce an enterprise-wide minimum protection level** even when project teams create their own templates.

Use Model Armor floor settings only for Google Cloud Gemini apps and leave other-cloud apps to team-specific filters.

questions.title: Assessing enterprise-app controls against country-specific requirements
questions.prompt:
Hanmaeum Accounting has offices in Korea and Germany. It uses Claude Enterprise company-wide, while the German office also uses a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace with EU data residency. Compliance must satisfy all these internal rules:

- Rule 1: German audit work occurs entirely inside Claude projects. Conversations must be deleted after 90 days, and auditors must be able to verify deletion.
- Rule 2: When employees enter client financial data into Claude, the internal DLP engine must block it **before model processing**.
- Rule 3: Investigations of former employees must be able to obtain their **conversation content** up to 120 days after departure.
- Rule 4: **Data from every app** used in the German workspace must not be stored outside the EU.

For each proposed control, select **Yes if it meets its rule while also complying with the other rules, or No otherwise**.

1. For Rule 1, set both chat and project retention to 90 days in Claude Enterprise custom retention and verify deletion through audit-log deletion events.
2. For Rule 2, enable Claude Enterprise inference hooks (beta), having the internal DLP server allow or deny every prompt and tool call.
3. For Rule 3, retain Rule 1's 90-day setting and have the Primary Owner export the employee's conversation content when an investigation starts.
4. For Rule 4, because apps without sync support in the workspace region do not fall back to storage elsewhere, allow all apps without individual review, including apps without sync.

items.text: For Rule 1, set both chat and project retention to 90 days in Claude Enterprise custom retention and verify deletion through audit-log deletion events.
For Rule 2, enable Claude Enterprise inference hooks (beta), having the internal DLP server allow or deny every prompt and tool call.
For Rule 3, retain Rule 1's 90-day setting and have the Primary Owner export the employee's conversation content when an investigation starts.
For Rule 4, because apps without sync support in the workspace region do not fall back to storage elsewhere, allow all apps without individual review, including apps without sync.

questions.explanation:
Mapping rules to controls requires checking not just whether a feature exists but whether its scope covers the requirement and conflicts with another rule's settings. All four proposals use real capabilities, but proposal 3 conflicts with Rule 1 and proposal 4 has narrower coverage than required.

- **1 (Yes)**: Chats within projects follow project retention, not chat retention, and projects default to indefinite retention, so both must be set to 90 days. Retention changes and deletion events are recorded in audit logs, enabling verification.
- **2 (Yes)**: Inference hooks are an Enterprise beta that sends prompts to a customer server before generation and tool calls before execution, proceeding only after an allow/deny response. Owners and Primary Owners enable and manage them.
- **3 (No)**: Primary Owner data export is the correct route to conversation content, but under 90-day retention, conversations older than 90 days after departure have already been deleted and cannot be exported. Audit logs contain events and identifiers, not conversation content, and cannot substitute. Meeting 120 days requires reconciling Rule 1, for example a separate preservation process for investigation holds.
- **4 (No)**: It is true that unsupported sync regions do not fall back to storage elsewhere, but apps without sync follow third-party providers' storage, processing, and residency terms. Workspace data residency does not cover third-party apps, so each requires review.

Additional note: Shortening retention immediately schedules out-of-window data for deletion when saved, and it cannot be recovered.

Both send `temperature: 0.2`. Anthropic announced the model's deprecation on September 30, 2026. The platform team wants **no service interruption**. Which plan is most appropriate?

Audit usage through Console exports, use Claude API’s November 30 retirement as a shared deadline, and switch both paths together to `claude-sonnet-5-5` without `temperature` that day.
Audit usage through Console exports, migrate Claude API to `claude-sonnet-5-5` without `temperature` before November 30, and migrate Google Cloud according to its own retirement schedule.

- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It includes auditing, predeadline migration, parameter changes, and path-specific schedules. The tradeoff is separate migration timing and validation.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Retired-model requests fail, and the retained `temperature: 0.2` causes 400 errors on the replacement too, interrupting service.

questions.title: Migrating to Responses while preserving portability
questions.prompt:
Barun Insurance runs Chat Completions-based support in a ZDR-approved OpenAI organization and wants Responses for reasoning models. Requirements:

- **Maintain ZDR**.
- Keep conversation state **in company storage** so history remains reusable after a future provider migration.
- Preserve reasoning context across turns.
- Migrate existing function tools with **minimal behavioral changes**; some schemas are incompatible with strict mode.

Select **2** actions.

options.text: Continue with `previous_response_id`, sending only new messages, and store response IDs and user messages internally for later reconstruction.
Keep state in Conversations API objects for reasoning continuity and export weekly to company storage for portability.
Call with `store: false`; store each turn’s output items, including reasoning items containing `encrypted_content`, internally and include them in the next input.
Keep Chat Completions function definitions nested under `function` and omit `strict` to retain existing behavior.
Move function definitions to top-level `name`, `description`, and `parameters`, explicitly setting `strict: false` to retain nonstrict behavior.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are ZDR, company-owned state, and minimal behavior changes. OpenAI's migration guide says ZDR organizations cannot use stateful Responses and automatically receive `store: false`. Retain and resend returned reasoning items for continuity. Responses function definitions use top-level fields; omitting `strict` attempts strict mode, so explicitly use `strict: false` to preserve behavior.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Provider-side state continuation conflicts with ZDR stateless operation. Storing only user messages omits model outputs and reasoning items, violating portability. All prior continued input tokens are also billed as input.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: It preserves reasoning and backups, but Conversations is not ZDR-eligible and retains data until deletion.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Stateless calls and reasoning-item resubmission satisfy ZDR, portability, and continuity.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: Chat Completions nests definitions under `function`; Responses uses top-level fields, so unchanged definitions are incompatible. Omitting `strict` also attempts strict mode and changes behavior.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Even strict-incompatible schemas retain their previous nonstrict behavior.

Additional note: Chat Completions remains supported, allowing gradual feature-by-feature migration without deadline pressure. Even with `previous_response_id`, top-level `instructions` do not carry over and must be resent each request.

- (3) Share the plugin with the existing user group or publish it in the workspace directory.
- (4) Check one target-department user’s Use plugins permission and installation policy, share only with that user, and ask them to install and test.
- (5) Have the GPT author or workspace administrator run Migrate to plugin from My GPTs.

items.text: Replace nonmigrated custom actions by connecting a claims-system custom MCP server to the plugin, and separately compare-test it against the original action.
Correct the identified instructions in the GPT editor and publish them together with outstanding draft changes.
Share the plugin with the existing user group or publish it in the workspace directory.
Check one target-department user’s Use plugins permission and installation policy, share only with that user, and ask them to install and test.
Have the GPT author or workspace administrator run Migrate to plugin from My GPTs.

questions.explanation:
The sequence follows migration dependencies. Migration uses only the latest published version and makes the original GPT read-only. Fixing instructions only in the plugin afterward cannot satisfy both-original-and-new correctness. New plugins start private, are not automatically installed/shared, and do not inherit custom actions or sharing settings. Enterprise guidance recommends reviewing/testing before sharing and asking target users to install/test.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Basis |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (2) Fix instructions and publish drafts | Starting point; originals cannot be edited after migration. | Only the latest published version migrates, excluding drafts. Originals remain usable until retirement but become read-only. |
| 2 | (5) Run migration | Uses the published version from (2). | Authors or workspace admins can migrate published GPTs; usage permission alone is insufficient. |
| 3 | (1) Rebuild actions and compare-test | Requires the plugin created in (5). | Custom actions do not migrate and need replacements such as custom MCP servers. Rebuilt integration must be separately tested, not assumed equivalent. |
| 4 | (4) One-user installation/test | Tests the complete claims-enabled plugin from (1). | Users need Use plugins and installation permission, or admin installation. Private-by-default plugins must be explicitly shared with the tester. |
| 5 | (3) Group sharing/directory publication | Exposure depends on verification in (4). | Sharing settings do not migrate; existing users gain no automatic access, so reshare after verification. |

Additional note: Enterprise creation of new custom GPTs is scheduled to stop October 26; publish drafts to migrate before then. Share plugins permission is needed for people/groups; Publish plugins to workspace is separately needed for the directory. Only approved deferred workspaces may continue until February 11, 2027, so do not assume an extension.

questions.title: Which group-wide release standard is most appropriate?
questions.context:
> [Company overview] Hanul Financial Group has banking, card, and insurance units in Korea, Singapore, and Germany. The group AI platform team approves generative-AI releases across all three.
>
> [Existing environment] Banking uses OpenAI API, cards Claude API, and insurance Gemini on Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform for customer support. Banking has collected evaluation results in the OpenAI Evals dashboard for group reporting.
>
> [Requirement 1] Apply **one release standard** to all three units, independent of provider and reapplied whenever models/prompts change. Also thoroughly validate **unit-specific high-risk tasks**, such as accurately explaining insurance clauses.
>
> [Requirement 2] Continuously monitor production quality and safety compliance after release, rolling back if standards are missed. Group reporting must continue **without interruption beyond 2027**.
>
> [Operational constraints] Two expert reviewers can jointly review only about 200 cases per week. The card unit plans a new-model migration **within three weeks**. Production LLM-grading costs must stay **within a monthly budget**.
>
> [Security requirements] A risk committee member proposes: "All three providers maintain public safety frameworks, including Anthropic RSP and Google DeepMind's Frontier Safety Framework, so we can skip our own adversarial testing."

options.text: Build a shared evaluation set from production logs, add division-specific high-risk and adversarial cases such as jailbreaks, and use one passing threshold of at least 4.0 from human review. Have the two expert reviewers grade the entire set on every model or prompt change.

Build a shared evaluation set from production logs with division-specific high-risk and adversarial cases such as jailbreaks, and run an LLM grader calibrated with human labels on every change. Let divisions retain their own passing thresholds, with the release committee comparing results side by side.

Build a shared evaluation set and one pass/fail standard from production logs, add division-specific high-risk and adversarial cases such as jailbreaks, and run an LLM grader on every change. Have expert reviewers label only a sample to check agreement and calibrate the grader.

Build a shared evaluation set from production logs with division-specific high-risk cases, use a human-calibrated LLM grader with a shared passing average of 80 for all divisions, and run it on every change. Omit adversarial cases because providers manage risks through safety frameworks.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are one release standard and division-specific high-risk tasks in Requirement 1, the roughly 200 reviews per week and three-week deadline in operational constraints, and the security requirement. OpenAI's evaluation guidance recommends task-specific evaluations reflecting real traffic, pass/fail criteria, and continuous evaluation on every change. Human evaluation offers the highest quality but is slow and expensive, so use LLM graders after validating agreement with human labels. Google Well-Architected AI/ML operational excellence also recommends predeployment adversarial testing to find vulnerabilities and failure modes. All options satisfy some needs, but only one simultaneously meets a single standard, staffing and schedule limits, and adversarial validation. The tradeoff is reviewer time for initial sample labeling and some grader error.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; overengineered)**: The shared standard and adversarial cases are appropriate, but two people grading the entire set on every change exceed the 200-per-week limit and the card division's three-week schedule. The guidance recommends calibrating automated grading with human judgment rather than abandoning it.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Automated calibrated grading and high-risk/adversarial cases are present, but division-specific thresholds violate one release standard and hinder cross-division comparison.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: One standard, division-specific high-risk and adversarial cases, and automated grading calibrated with a small human-labeled sample make repeated evaluation feasible within staffing and schedule limits.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; confuses related capabilities)**: A shared standard, calibrated grader, and schedule compliance are present, but the security proposal is a distractor. RSP and the Frontier Safety Framework manage severe risks of providers' frontier models by capability level; they do not replace testing vulnerabilities specific to Hanul's service context.

questions.title: Per-developer spending caps and SSO for Claude Code on Bedrock
questions.prompt:
Hanbit Motors wants 500 developers to use Claude Code. Requirements:

- Run inference on Amazon Bedrock in the company's AWS account for data-location and contractual requirements.
- Set individual spending caps and **immediately block** requests from developers who exceed them.
- Developers sign in with the corporate IdP and **never receive API keys or AWS credentials directly**.
- The platform team wants as few new servers to operate as possible.

The first three requirements are mandatory; the last is negotiable. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Assign Claude Enterprise seats to all developers and set individual spending limits for usage credits, using corporate SSO and individual blocking.

Have developers call Bedrock directly with their own AWS credentials, export individual token/cost metrics through OpenTelemetry, and address overages through AWS budget alerts and month-end reconciliation.
Self-host an open-source LLM gateway in front of Bedrock, issue virtual keys per developer to track spending, and have operations manually reconcile overages.
Self-host Claude apps gateway in front of Bedrock, require IdP login, and set per-developer monthly spending caps that block over-limit requests.

questions.explanation:

Claude Code documentation describes Claude apps gateway as a self-hosted service placed in front of cloud providers such as Bedrock. Developers sign in with the corporate IdP without holding API keys or cloud credentials. Spending limits can be daily, weekly, or monthly at developer, group, or organization level; the next request after a developer exceeds a limit is blocked with 429. The tradeoffs are operating the gateway and PostgreSQL limit store, and reconciling estimated gateway amounts with provider usage reports rather than treating them as invoices. The default allows requests when the store is unreachable; guaranteed blocking requires fail-closed behavior, making store outages inference outages. The documentation notes that Claude Enterprise may fit better when SCIM provisioning or web/mobile Claude Code is needed.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Can provide SSO and individual limits, but inference runs at Anthropic, violating [inference on Bedrock]. The documentation directs organizations requiring their own cloud path to apps gateway.

questions.title: Initially exposing a claims-system app as read-only
questions.prompt:
Hangyeol Insurance's IT team connected an internal claims-system app to ChatGPT Enterprise. At connection time, four read actions and two write actions (changing claim status and registering payment approval) were already enabled. The new-action policy automatically allows new actions. Requirements and constraints:

- Open read access to **all employees this quarter**.
- **Nobody may execute write actions before audit review is complete**; the review organization will be formed next quarter.
- If the provider adds new actions during review, **they must not become enabled before review**.
- Business teams want write automation quickly, but there is no staff to operate temporary exceptions.

How should the three app-control layers—who can use it, which actions are allowed, and when confirmation is requested—be combined?

options.text: Open the app to all employee roles and leave all actions, including writes, enabled; set Permissions to ask every time so writes run only after user confirmation.
Open the app only to claims-handling roles for limited read/write use, then expand to all employees after review next quarter.
Open the app to all employees and individually disable the two existing write actions, leaving reads only; retain the current automatic-allow policy for new actions.
Open the app to all employees, individually disable the two existing writes, and enable the policy that disables new actions. Re-enable writes individually after review and choose Permissions then.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [nobody can write before review] and [new actions must remain off before review]. OpenAI's help article distinguishes Role access (who uses an app), Actions (what it can do), and Permissions (when ChatGPT requests confirmation). The policy disabling new actions applies only to subsequently introduced actions; it does not disable actions already enabled, so existing writes must be turned off individually. The correct approach meets early rollout and audit requirements at the cost of delaying write automation until next quarter and administering action-by-action reactivation.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: confusing related controls)**: Reads can roll out immediately, but Permissions controls when confirmation is requested, not whether an action is allowed. Enabled writes can execute before review if a user approves, violating audit constraints.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Reduces write exposure by narrowing Role access, but fails to open reads to [all employees this quarter].
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Blocks current writes, but automatically enables provider-added actions during review. The new-action policy is not retroactive and must be enabled separately from disabling existing actions.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Uses Role access for all-employee reads, the Actions layer to disable existing writes, and the new-action policy to block future additions. The tradeoffs are a quarter's delay in write automation and reactivation/per-action review work.

Also note: Provider-side OAuth-scope approval is separate from ChatGPT action activation; approving scopes does not automatically enable new actions. These app permissions apply to ChatGPT conversations, while workspace agents have separate agent-specific controls.

- (2) Separate staging and production projects and restrict access to production.
- (3) Before expiry, issue a replacement key, apply it to the app, verify operation, then revoke the old key.

items.text: Issue a service-account key with an expiry date in the production project and register it in the app's secret store.

Before expiry, issue a replacement key, apply it to the app, verify operation, then revoke the old key.
