Spending is measured at list price and updates take about two hours, allowing overages. Bedrock has a separate capacity pool and retains AWS billing, but lacks Batches, Files API, and Skills, and negotiated discounts do not transfer. The correct answer sacrifices automated allocation, accepts 1.1× pricing and possible overages, and cannot fail over every service.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Enforces geography at workspace level, allows budget headroom to reduce interruption risk, and limits failover to overlapping real-time features.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Code-level parameters can be omitted, letting a call use global and failing to enforce US-only inference.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Preserves features and all-service failover, but shifts billing directly to Anthropic, violating retained AWS invoicing.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Strict budget alignment causes request failures at the limit, with delayed spending updates, violating uninterrupted essential service requirements.

**References**: [Claude Platform on AWS](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-platform-on-aws) · [Claude Data residency](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency) · [Claude in Amazon Bedrock](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-in-amazon-bedrock)

questions.title: Central control of developer-tool calls to internal agents
questions.prompt:
Security wants Agent Gateway to centrally control calls from developers' Claude Code and Gemini CLI to internal agents. Some agents are deployed on Agent Runtime and others operate in Gemini Enterprise. Constraints:

- Centrally control **incoming calls from developer tools**.
- **Minimize redeployment and migration** of existing agents.
- Keep Gemini Enterprise agents in place for employee work.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Redeploy all agents on Agent Runtime, including those from Gemini Enterprise, and place all behind Client-to-Agent gateways for one control approach.
Configure an Agent-to-Anywhere gateway to control agents' outbound calls and use that to handle developer-tool inbound calls as well.
Distribute allowed-agent lists in Claude Code and Gemini CLI configuration files on developer PCs, with security updating lists quarterly.
Apply Client-to-Agent gateways to Agent Runtime agents; exclude Gemini Enterprise agents and use them only through the employee-app path.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [incoming developer-tool calls] and [minimize redeployment/migration]. Agent Gateway distinguishes Client-to-Agent ingress from Agent-to-Anywhere egress. Agent Runtime supports both, but Gemini Enterprise supports egress only, not Client-to-Agent. The tradeoff is leaving Gemini Enterprise agents outside central ingress control.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Completes ingress coverage but requires redeploying every Gemini Enterprise agent, violating minimal migration.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: confusing related features)**: Egress controls calls leaving agents, not developer-tool inbound calls, violating the first constraint.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Avoids migration, but control is distributed across developer PCs rather than central.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Applies ingress control where supported and restricts the use of unsupported agents without moving them.

**References**: [Agent Gateway overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/gateways/agent-gateway-overview)

questions.title: Allowing only read tools on a remote MCP server
questions.prompt:
Business-unit agents call an approved remote MCP server run by another organization. The server provides both read and write tools. Security wants Agent Gateway to enforce:

- Agents may call **read tools only**; write calls must be blocked.
- The server belongs to another organization, so **server-side changes cannot be requested**.
- Manage controls **centrally**, not in agent code.

Which control is most appropriate?

options.text: Register the MCP server in Agent Registry and use tool attributes as authorization-policy conditions to allow only read tools.
Create an IAM policy allowing the entire server URL, and instruct each business-unit agent not to call write tools.
Ask the server owner to operate a separate read-only copy with write tools removed, and allow only that copy.
Add allowed-tool filters to each business unit's agent code to block write calls before execution.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [read tools only] and [central management]. For MCP traffic, Agent Gateway parses requests to extract attributes and can use them in authorization policies to allow specific tools. Registering targets in Agent Registry is recommended for fine-grained controls such as tool-level rules; unregistered targets require explicit URL-targeted IAM policies to connect.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Enforces tool-level access at one gateway without modifying the server.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: URL-level permission opens the entire server; instructions are not enforcement and cannot guarantee blocked write calls.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Effective, but violates the no-server-change constraint and adds duplicate-server operations.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Can block per tool, but requires changing code in every unit rather than central management.

Also note: Tool-level rules apply only to MCP traffic, not other protocols.

**References**: [Agent Gateway overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/gateways/agent-gateway-overview)

questions.title: Preventing unapproved new tools from appearing on a shared MCP server
questions.prompt:
An internal Claude API app uses MCP connector tools from a shared remote MCP server operated by another team. New tools are frequently added, and existing descriptions/schemas change. Requirements:

- Tools **must not be exposed to the model before security review**.
- **Later changes to approved definitions must not take effect before re-review**.
- Reviews occur **once a week**; business teams want immediate access to new tools.
- Keep the Messages API call structure; there is no staff to operate a separate MCP-client service.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: List only risky tools with `enabled: false` in `mcp_toolset` configs and expose everything else as returned by the server.
Set `enabled: false` in `mcp_toolset.default_config`, enabling only approved tools in configs. Accept their latest server-returned definitions on every call, adding new tools after weekly review.
Set default `enabled` to false and enable only approved tools; use the 2026-09-15 beta header to record and pin the tool list. Update new tools and changes after weekly review.
Avoid MCP connector; have the backend connect through a client-side MCP helper and convert only approved tools into Messages API tools. Apply definition changes during weekly review.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [no exposure before review] and [no definition changes before re-review]. Setting `enabled: false` in `mcp_toolset.default_config` enables only tools named in configs, so newly added tools stay disabled: an allowlist. Disabling individual tools without a default config is a denylist, leaving new tools enabled by default. The `mcp-client-2026-09-15` beta header permits recording and pinning the server-returned tool list; once pinned, the API does not ask the server again. The tradeoff is up to a week's delay for new/changed tools.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Simplest configuration, but the denylist exposes new tools before review.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Blocks new tools but immediately accepts changed descriptions/schemas of approved tools, violating definition stability.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Combines an allowlist with a pinned tool list, updating only after weekly review.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: overengineering)**: Gives the app direct control of exposure/definitions but requires operating MCP-client connections, violating staffing limits. Client-side helpers fit local STDIO servers or cases requiring direct connection management.

Also note: MCP connector is not ZDR-eligible; exchanged tool definitions/results follow standard retention. The 2026-09-15 header is available on Claude API. Connector is beta and header names may change; this follows documentation as of October 16, 2026.

**References**: [MCP connector](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector)

questions.title: Checks before Google Drive sync in an EU-residency workspace
questions.prompt: IT plans admin-managed Google Drive sync in a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace configured for EU data residency. Three requirements apply: **no storage outside the EU**, **no expansion beyond members' original file-access permissions**, and **a pilot limited to one Legal-team folder**. Choose **two checks/actions** before the pilot.

options.text: First check the regional-support table for EU sync support for this app and connection type; do not create the connection if unsupported.
While verifying EU sync, create a temporary US-residency workspace and start the Legal-folder pilot there.
Because source Drive permissions remain effective in search after sync, review the Legal folder's sharing settings and restrict sync to that folder.
Sync all of Drive at once, relying on source permissions in search to naturally hide content from employees outside Legal.
Move the Legal folder to a shared drive visible to all employees before syncing, aligning source permissions with search-result access.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [no storage outside the EU] and [one Legal folder only]. OpenAI's help article says sync availability depends on the app, admin-managed connection type, and workspace data region. Unsupported regional sync does not automatically fall back to storage elsewhere. Source access permissions remain effective after sync, and Drive sources can be restricted to specified shared drives or folders.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Checks regional eligibility first, eliminating the possibility of storing outside the EU.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Accelerates the pilot but stores data outside the EU, violating the first requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Reviews access based on preserved source permissions and narrows sync to the Legal folder, meeting the third requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Preserved permissions prevent expanded access, but syncing unnecessary files violates the single-folder pilot scope.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Eliminates permission mismatch by expanding access to everyone, violating access preservation.

**References**: [Admin controls, security, and compliance in connectors (Enterprise, Edu, and Business)](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11509118-admin-controls-security-and-compliance-in-connectors-enterprise-edu-and-business)

questions.title: EU SharePoint ingestion and CMEK in Gemini Enterprise
questions.prompt:
A team wants to ingest a business unit's SharePoint documents into Gemini Enterprise in the EU. Requirements:

- Keep data in **the EU region**.
- Use **customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK)**.
- SharePoint is **a third-party data source**, not a Google source.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Create the data store in the EU multi-region location and attach only an EU multi-region key, treating SharePoint like a Google source.
Create the data store in the EU multi-region location and create and attach both EU multi-region and single-region keys.
Choose global and attach a single regional key to simplify key management.
Create the data store in the EU multi-region location but use default Google-owned/managed encryption instead of CMEK, removing key checks from the checklist.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [CMEK] and [third-party source]. Gemini Enterprise documents mandatory encryption for data ingested into US/EU locations, using Google-owned/managed keys by default with optional CMEK. With CMEK, Google sources require a multi-region key; third-party sources require both multi-region and single-region keys. CMEK is supported only through US/EU multi-region APIs, not global.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Fits a Google source but omits the single-region key required for third-party SharePoint.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Meets EU placement, CMEK, and third-party key requirements at the cost of managing two key types.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Simplifies management, but global lacks CMEK support and violates EU placement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Meets EU and encryption requirements but not CMEK.

**References**: [Introduction to connectors and data stores](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/connectors/introduction-to-connectors-and-data-stores) · [Gemini Enterprise compliance and security controls](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini/enterprise/docs/compliance-security-controls)

questions.title: Claude workspaces for business-unit caps and shared-prefix caching
questions.prompt:
An enterprise AI team wants Sales, Logistics, Finance, and HR to share one Claude API organization. Requirements:

- **Enforce** each unit's monthly spending cap on Anthropic's side.
- Set per-unit rate limits so one unit's traffic surge does not consume others' throughput.
- Automatically produce per-unit cost reports from **one organization**.
- All four units use the same roughly 15,000-token policy prefix; share its cache between units to reduce input costs if possible.

The first three requirements are mandatory; the last is optional. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Create a workspace per unit with spending/rate limits, cache the prefix separately in each workspace, and group cost reports by workspace.
Use one shared workspace and shared prefix cache, distinguish units by API keys, and allocate monthly costs from key-level usage.
Issue per-unit API keys in the Default Workspace, set limits only once at organization level, and allocate costs using key-level usage reports.
Create a separate Claude organization per unit with organization-specific spending/rate limits and separately cached prefixes.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [Anthropic-enforced per-unit caps] and [reporting from one organization]. Claude documentation defines spending and rate limits at workspace level, set only below organization limits; overall organization limits always apply. Cost reports can group by workspace. Prompt caches are isolated by workspace in Claude API, requiring separate prefix writes/reads per unit. Files, batches, and skills are also workspace-scoped, so shared assets must be uploaded per unit. The correct answer pays repeated cache-write costs for every unit.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Meets all three mandatory requirements while sacrificing cache sharing.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Shares cache, but workspace-level limits cannot enforce separate unit caps/rates inside one shared workspace.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Documentation says limits cannot be configured on the Default Workspace, so per-unit spending/rate limits cannot be applied.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Enforces organization-level limits but violates single-organization reporting, with no cache-sharing benefit across organizations.

**References**: [Workspaces](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/workspaces) · [Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Rate limits](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits) · [Usage and Cost API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/usage-cost-api)

questions.title: Gateway design for both Claude API and Bedrock
questions.prompt:
A platform team places its own gateway in front of several models and calls Claude through both Claude API and Amazon Bedrock. Requirements:

- **Keep both paths** for redundancy.
- When a model refuses a request, **retry through an alternative model consistently on both paths**.
- **Show refusals in the operations dashboard**.

Choose **two mandatory design elements**.

options.text: On the Bedrock path, return refusals directly to callers without fallback retries.
Monitor refusals only through HTTP 4xx/5xx error-rate alerts.
Configure server-side `fallbacks` for Claude API and SDK client-side fallback middleware for Bedrock.
Remove Bedrock and standardize on Claude API server-side fallbacks to simplify operations and eliminate configuration differences.
Because refusals are successful responses, separately measure the proportion of responses with `stop_reason` equal to `refusal` in the dashboard.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [consistent alternative-model retries on both paths] and [visible in operations dashboards]. Server-side `fallbacks` is beta on Claude API and unavailable for Message Batches API, Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud, or Microsoft Foundry; documentation recommends SDK middleware for client-side fallback on those platforms. Refusals are successful HTTP 200 responses with `stop_reason: refusal`, so error-rate/5xx monitoring misses them.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Retains Bedrock but lacks retry behavior, violating path consistency.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Reuses existing monitoring, but refusals are 200 responses rather than errors and remain invisible.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Uses each path's supported mechanism to align retry behavior. Do not combine server fallbacks and middleware on the same request.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Aligns behavior by sacrificing a redundancy path, violating the first requirement.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Counting by `stop_reason` exposes refusals.

**References**: [Refusals and fallback](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback)

questions.title: Automatic Fable 5.1 refusal fallback including nested calls
questions.prompt:
A platform gateway must automatically retry refused Claude Fable 5.1 requests with an allowed alternative model. The app also makes nested model calls inside agent-tool execution. Requirements:

- Retry automatically **without showing refusals as errors to users**.
- Apply the same fallback to **nested model calls inside agents**.
- An external agent framework creates nested requests, and **their request parameters cannot be changed**. The team does create the SDK client object passed to that framework.
- **Do not combine server-side fallbacks and SDK middleware on the same request**. Prefer concentrating gateway code changes in one place.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Set server-side `fallbacks` to "default" on gateway-created requests and leave nested agent calls unchanged.
Install fallback middleware on both the gateway SDK client and the client passed to the framework; do not use server-side fallbacks.
Set server-side fallbacks on gateway requests and directly add the fallbacks parameter to nested requests.
Send requests through a middleware-enabled client while also setting server-side fallbacks on those same requests.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are [nested calls also need fallback] and [request parameters cannot be changed]. Server-side `fallbacks` does not propagate to model calls inside tool execution and must be configured separately on every request path. Middleware and server-side fallbacks serve the same purpose, so only one should be used per request. Middleware attaches to the client object, covering nested calls without modifying framework-created parameters. The tradeoff is spreading changes across multiple clients rather than one place. If the fallback model cannot read the previous model's thinking blocks, they are removed, potentially increasing cost and latency while replanning on the first turn after switching.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Centralizes changes but server-side settings do not propagate to nested calls, leaving them without fallback.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Client-level middleware covers both gateway and nested calls.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Matches the documented per-path configuration approach, but violates the inability to modify framework request parameters.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect: constraint violation)**: Broadens coverage but violates both the documentation and scenario's prohibition on combining mechanisms for one request.

Also note: Server-side fallbacks are beta and available only on Claude API. Client-side middleware serves platforms such as Bedrock that lack server-side support. These statements follow the reference-date documentation; header values may change.

**References**: [Refusals and fallback](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback) · [Claude Fable 5.1 migration guide](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/fable-5-1/migration-guide)

questions.title: Preserving cache savings after switching to Gemini 3.8 Flash
questions.prompt: A business-unit app has been creating a cached_content object from an internal policy manual of about 20,000 tokens and referencing it in every request. It is switching to Gemini 3.8 Flash, then plans to migrate to the Interactions API and upgrade to newer-generation models (Gemini 4 Argon and later). Choose TWO configuration changes that preserve cache savings **without abandoning the planned migration**.

options.text: Remove code that creates and references cached_content, and keep shared material such as the manual fixed at the beginning of prompts to enable implicit cache hits.
Postpone the Interactions API migration and continue explicit caching with generateContent; also postpone newer-generation model upgrades until explicit-cache support is confirmed.
Rebuild relevant policy excerpts for each question and place them at the beginning of the prompt.
Add monitoring of total_cached_tokens in response usage information to check cache hits, and account for the absence of retention-time control and guaranteed hits in cost forecasts.
Spread requests across different times to increase the intervals between them.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are migration to the Interactions API, upgrades to Gemini 4 Argon and later, and not abandoning the planned migration. Gemini documentation states that explicit caching, where cache objects are created and managed directly, is unsupported in the Interactions API and unavailable on Gemini 4 Argon and later models. Implicit caching is enabled without additional configuration. Placing large shared content at the start of prompts and sending requests with similar prefixes within a short time window improves hits, which are reported in usage.total_cached_tokens. The tradeoff is losing retention-time control and guaranteed cache hits.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: This is the essential move to implicit caching, which remains available with the new models and API.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It preserves savings but abandons the Interactions API migration, and the approach is unavailable on later model generations, violating the migration requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; approach for another situation)**: Changing the prefix for every question breaks the shared prefix, reducing implicit-cache hits and eliminating savings.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Implicit-cache hits must be verified through metrics, and operations must account for the lack of retention-time control.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; approach for another situation)**: Wider request intervals contradict the recommendation to send similar prefixes within a short window and reduce hits.

**References**: [Gemini API Context caching](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching)

questions.title: Evaluating an Admin and Rate Limits API design for automated limit checks
questions.prompt:
A Claude API organization’s platform team is designing automated checks of business-unit workspace limits. There are three requirements: **the script only reads limits**, while humans approve changes; it checks **all workspaces, including Default Workspace**; and **only one organization-level credential set** is maintained. Mark each design decision Yes if it is factually consistent with these requirements, or No otherwise.

1. Automate limit reads with the Rate Limits API, while a human changes values on the Console’s Rate limits page.
2. Read Default Workspace overrides with the same script by adding include_inherited=true to the workspace endpoint.
3. Treat model groups absent from the workspace response’s data as having no overrides, and use organization limits for those groups.
4. Distribute each business unit’s workspace API key as the script’s credentials, without creating separate organization-level administrative credentials.

items.text: Automate limit reads with the Rate Limits API, while a human changes values on the Console’s Rate limits page.
Read Default Workspace overrides with the same script by adding include_inherited=true to the workspace endpoint.
Treat model groups absent from the workspace response’s data as having no overrides, and use organization limits for those groups.
Distribute each business unit’s workspace API key as the script’s credentials, without creating separate organization-level administrative credentials.

questions.explanation:
For Admin APIs, separately check read/write capabilities, workspace scope, credential types, and what missing results mean. The decisive requirements are read-only access, inclusion of Default Workspace, and one organization-level credential set.

- **1 (Yes)**: The documentation answers “No” to whether limits can be set through the Rate Limits API and directs users to edit workspace limits on the Console’s Rate limits page. This meets the read-only requirement.
- **2 (No)**: Default Workspace cannot have limit overrides, so this endpoint returns 404 regardless of include_inherited. Read its limits through the organization endpoint.
- **3 (Yes)**: A missing group has no workspace override. It inherits the organization-level limit rather than having unlimited capacity.
- **4 (No)**: The documentation allows Admin API keys, OAuth tokens with org:admin scope, and personal or service-account keys not bound to a workspace. Workspace API keys do not work. Organization-level credentials are required.

Also note: For claude.ai Enterprise organizations, only some Admin API endpoints, such as members and invitations, apply. Usage and cost require a separate Analytics API key.

**References**: [Rate Limits API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/rate-limits-api) · [Administration API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/administration-api) · [Usage and Cost API](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/usage-cost-api)

questions.title: Centralizing agent controls while retaining an internal policy engine
questions.prompt: An internal policy engine already decides whether tool calls are allowed, and auditing is tied to it. The security team wants to centralize agent controls through Agent Gateway while **keeping decisions in the existing policy engine** and **avoiding changes to agent code**. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.text: Use the gateway’s custom authorization engine capability through Service Extensions to delegate authorization decisions to the internal policy engine.
Add the policy engine’s SDK to each agent so the agent requests a decision before calling tools.
Rewrite all policy-engine rules as gateway IAM policies and retire the existing engine.
Skip the gateway and operate a custom proxy in front of the policy engine, routing all external agent calls through it to centralize decisions and audits.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are retaining the existing policy engine as the decision-maker and avoiding agent-code changes. Agent Gateway supports custom authorization engines through Service Extensions to delegate authorization decisions to third-party systems; these are managed through authorization policies. Features such as unified IAM-based access control and Model Armor can be added as needed.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It centralizes the control point at the gateway without changing who makes decisions.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: The policy engine still decides, but every agent requires code changes, violating the no-code-change requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Control is centralized, but IAM becomes the decision-maker and the policy engine is separated from auditing, violating the first condition.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: It retains the policy engine but gives up gateway-based centralized control and adds the burden of operating a custom proxy.

**References**: [Agent Gateway overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/gateways/agent-gateway-overview)

questions.title: Diagnosing why employees cannot use an enabled SharePoint app
questions.prompt: The IT help desk, which administers a ChatGPT Enterprise workspace, has enabled the SharePoint app. The plugin installation policy is “Available,” but many members cannot use the app. Microsoft Entra global administration belongs to the security team, a different organization from the help desk. Choose TWO correct checks or actions.

options.text: Change the plugin installation policy to “Installed” so it is installed for all members by default.
Check whether the Entra administrator (the security team) has granted organization-wide consent for the required Microsoft Graph permissions, and request that consent if it is missing.
Repeatedly request the app provider’s OAuth scope approval in ChatGPT administration until it is complete, then ask members to reopen the app.
Assume Entra consent is complete and ask members to retry without any other action.

After Entra consent, also check that the workspace administrator enabled the required SharePoint actions, and instruct members to connect their individual accounts if the app requires account linking.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are that the security team is the Entra global administrator, and that members cannot use the app despite the plugin being Available. OpenAI Help says some SharePoint actions require a Microsoft Entra administrator to grant organization-wide consent for Microsoft Graph permissions; that person may differ from the ChatGPT administrator. Consent does not enable ChatGPT actions or connect individual accounts, so workspace action enablement and member account linking remain separate steps. Plugin installation and app access are also separate controls.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; confusing similar features)**: Installation policy controls plugin installation, not access to its included apps. An installed plugin can still contain an inaccessible app.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It checks the first step while recognizing that the approving administrator may be different.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; approach for another situation)**: Provider-scope approval, action enablement, and Entra organization consent are separate checks. Repeating one does not resolve the others.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Consent does not replace action enablement or individual account linking, so access can remain unavailable without further action.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: It checks the two remaining steps after consent: action enablement and account linking.

**References**: [Admin controls, security, and compliance in connectors (Enterprise, Edu, and Business)](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/11509118-admin-controls-security-and-compliance-in-connectors-enterprise-edu-and-business)

questions.title: Using an internal STDIO MCP server from a Platform on AWS app
questions.prompt:
Hansol Trading wants a Claude Platform on AWS app to use an STDIO MCP server for inventory lookup inside its corporate network. Requirements:

- **Do not expose the server to the internet.**
- Another team owns the server and frequently changes its tool logic, so **do not duplicate that logic in the app**.
- **Keep the app on Platform on AWS.**

Which connection approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Expose the server as a public HTTPS endpoint and specify its URL in the MCP connector.
Reimplement the server’s tool logic in application code and register it as ordinary function tools.
Build and operate a separate internal agent runtime that calls the server, and stop using Claude Platform on AWS.
Have a backend inside the corporate network connect to the server as an MCP client, and use the SDK’s client-side MCP helpers to convert and pass its tools.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are not exposing the server to the internet and not duplicating its logic in the app. The MCP connector targets remote servers publicly exposed through HTTPS URLs and cannot directly connect to local STDIO servers. For local servers or other cases requiring a custom MCP client connection, the documentation recommends the SDK’s client-side helpers. Platform on AWS also does not support MCP tunnels and supports only publicly exposed servers through that connection mechanism.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It works with the connector but requires public exposure, violating the first requirement.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It eliminates the connection problem but creates duplicate logic to maintain, violating the second requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It can access the server but abandons Platform on AWS, violating the third requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It keeps the server internal, reuses its logic, and preserves the Platform on AWS call structure. The tradeoff is that the backend must manage the MCP connection itself.

**References**: [MCP connector](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/mcp-connector) · [Claude Platform on AWS](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-platform-on-aws)

questions.title: Applying one shared personal-data masking policy across agents
questions.prompt: In a Gemini-based ADK service, five agents share one Runner. The security team wants **personal data in tool arguments masked by the same rules across all five agents**, with **only one place to change** when policy changes. The development schedule does not allow adding a new agent. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Put the same instruction against passing personal data to tools in all five system prompts, and inspect logs afterward for violations.
Register the PII Redaction plugin once on the App (Runner), applying it to tool calls from all five agents.
Write and attach a before-tool callback to each agent, with each agent owner managing masking rules separately.
Place an input-masking preprocessing function before the Runner, and leave tool arguments to the model’s judgment.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are the same rules for all five agents and one place to change them. ADK documentation recommends plugins registered once on the Runner (App in Python) for security policies spanning agents. Agent-specific callbacks suit logic confined to one agent. The PII Redaction plugin is designed to mask personal data before tools process or transmit it.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; confusing similar features)**: Instructions merely ask the model to comply; they do not deterministically enforce the same rules.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: One registration applies across agents and tool calls, with one modification point. The tradeoff is that agent-specific exceptions require additional callbacks.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It works, but distributes policy across five modification points and risks inconsistency.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; approach for another situation)**: Input masking is useful, but does not cover model-generated tool arguments or tool results, so it fails the requirement for arguments passed to tools.

**References**: [ADK Plugins](https://adk.dev/plugins/) · [ADK Safety and Security](https://adk.dev/safety/)

questions.title: Designing failover from Platform on AWS to a Bedrock backup
questions.prompt: A team uses Claude Platform on AWS as its primary Claude route and Amazon Bedrock as backup, and is designing failover in an enterprise gateway. Requirements: **normal requests use only the primary route**; failure switches to backup **without human intervention**; and routing logic stays **in the gateway without changes to individual service code**. Only real-time calls are in scope for redundancy. Choose TWO design considerations.

options.text: Implement client-side fallback in the gateway that detects primary-call errors and resends the same request to Bedrock.
Have each service implement both primary and Bedrock calls and switch routes independently during failure.
Split normal traffic equally between both routes to keep the backup warm, without separate failover logic.
Maintain per-route model-ID mappings in the gateway and translate to Bedrock-format model IDs when calling Bedrock.
Create a runbook requiring an operator to change gateway configuration to the backup when primary failure is confirmed.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are no human intervention and implementation in one gateway. Platform on AWS has a capacity pool separate from Bedrock, allowing the two routes to provide resilience. Bedrock uses separate model IDs with an `anthropic.` prefix and does not support the server-side fallbacks parameter; the documentation describes client-side fallback patterns. The gateway must therefore detect errors, retry, and translate model IDs.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It implements automatic failover in one gateway for a route combination that cannot use server-side fallback.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It switches automatically but requires each service to change code, violating the single-gateway requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: The backup stays warm, but normal requests use both routes, violating the primary-only requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: The gateway must absorb differences in model-ID formats for fallback calls to succeed.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: The procedure is controlled but requires human intervention, violating automatic failover.

**References**: [Claude Platform on AWS](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-platform-on-aws) · [Claude in Amazon Bedrock](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-in-amazon-bedrock) · [Refusals and fallback](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/refusals-and-fallback)

questions.title: What an owner can delegate to business-unit administrators
questions.prompt: A ChatGPT Enterprise workspace owner wants to **delegate business-unit member and group management to business administrators**, while **central IT retains billing and workspace-wide settings**. Which delegation approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Delegate group work along with billing settings and seat management so business administrators can handle everything in one place.
Delegate group work and permission to change workspace defaults, giving business units autonomy over settings.
Designate business administrators as group managers, delegate only selected group tasks, and retain billing, identity, seats, and defaults centrally.
Delegate workspace-name and image changes to business administrators while the owner retains other settings.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are delegating member/group management while retaining billing and global settings. Owners and administrators can delegate selected group tasks to group managers. This does not grant control over workspace-wide billing, identity, seat settings, or defaults. Only owners can change the workspace name and image.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Delegation does not transfer billing control and would also conflict with central retention.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Defaults are outside the delegation scope and must remain centrally controlled.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It delegates only the required tasks while preserving central controls. The tradeoff is that delegation is limited to selected group tasks.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; approach for another situation)**: Name and image changes are owner-only and cannot be delegated; they also do not address member-management delegation.

**References**: [Managing workspace settings in ChatGPT Enterprise](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/8411955-managing-workspace-settings-in-chatgpt-enterprise)

questions.title: Reconciling NGFW Enterprise inspection with Agent Gateway egress controls
questions.prompt:
Hanul Insurance’s Agent Platform agent (Agent Runtime) calls an external partner’s MCP server. Requirements:

- All external agent calls pass through **Agent Gateway egress**, blocking unregistered or unapproved destinations by default.
- Inspect tool-call payloads for sensitive-data leakage **in the request path**.
- The networking standard requires Cloud NGFW Enterprise inspection for all outbound traffic.
- Minimize the number of networks and gateways to manage.

The first two requirements are mandatory; the latter two may be relaxed. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Move the agent’s VPC to a network outside NGFW Enterprise inspection, apply Model Armor and IAM allow policies to Agent Gateway egress, and register the partner server.
Keep the existing NGFW Enterprise-inspected network and let the agent call the partner directly, combining NGFW domain allowlists with payload inspection in an internal proxy.
Use Agent Gateway egress and IAM allow policies in a separate VPC outside NGFW Enterprise, but inspect sensitive payload information afterward through weekly call-log reviews.
Configure Agent Gateway in Client-to-Agent mode to inspect incoming client requests with Model Armor, while keeping NGFW Enterprise network inspection.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are Agent Gateway egress routing and payload inspection in the request path. Agent Gateway documentation states that networks using Network Security Integration or Cloud NGFW Enterprise are unsupported: requests fail and Logging records 503. The NGFW Enterprise standard and gateway controls therefore cannot coexist on the same network. Egress mode is supported for Agent Runtime, denies connections by default without explicit IAM policies, and uses attached Model Armor to inspect tool payloads and agent responses for sensitive-data leakage. The correct choice requires approval for an exception from NGFW Enterprise standard inspection and operation of a separate network, replacing that inspection with Model Armor and IAM policies.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It preserves both mandatory requirements while relaxing the NGFW standard and network-count preference.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It preserves the NGFW standard but bypasses the gateway, violating the requirement that all external calls use gateway egress.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It preserves gateway control, but retrospective payload review fails the in-request-path requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; confusing similar features)**: Client-to-Agent mode handles inbound client-to-agent communication. Egress mode controls outbound agent calls. This does not satisfy either outbound-call control or its payload-inspection requirement.

Also note: With an agent connectivity template, traffic traverses a VPC network attachment, so VPC Service Controls perimeter rules apply.

**References**: [Agent Gateway overview](https://docs.cloud.google.com/gemini-enterprise-agent-platform/govern/gateways/agent-gateway-overview)

questions.title: Selecting a provider and caching configuration for a 3,000-token shared prefix
questions.prompt: A business-unit app prepends an internal policy manual of about 3,000 tokens to every request and makes dozens of calls per minute. Three requirements apply: **preserve the authoritative manual unchanged** (no summaries or additions), **reduce input costs**, and repeat calls **within five minutes**. OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini models are all allowed. Considering minimum cache lengths and pricing, which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Use Gemini 3.8 Flash and put the manual first in the prompt, expecting implicit caching to apply automatically.
Use Gemini 3.8 Flash, adding fixed examples after the manual to extend the prefix to at least 4,096 tokens.
Summarize the manual to at most 1,000 tokens to satisfy every provider’s minimum cache length.
Set a cache breakpoint on the manual with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and receive cache-read discounts on repeat calls within five minutes.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are preserving the authoritative manual unchanged and its 3,000-token length. Claude 5.5 models have a 512-token caching minimum, so the prefix qualifies. A five-minute cache write costs 1.25 times the base input rate, and Sonnet 5.5 cache reads cost 0.05 times that rate. Gemini 3.6/3.8 Flash implicit caching requires at least 4,096 tokens, so this prefix does not qualify. OpenAI GPT-5.6 and later require at least 1,024 tokens and would also qualify at this length, but this question focuses on minimum-length eligibility and preserving the original manual.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: The prefix is below the minimum, so caching does not apply and cannot deliver the required savings.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Caching becomes eligible, but content is added to the authoritative manual and the added tokens also cost money.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It may reduce costs, but violates preservation of the original manual.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It meets all three requirements. The tradeoffs are the initial 1.25-times write cost and reduced benefit if the cache is not reused within five minutes.

**References**: [Claude Prompt caching](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/prompt-caching) · [Gemini Context caching](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching) · [OpenAI Prompt caching](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/prompt-caching)

questions.title: Reordering a prompt to meet the implicit-cache minimum length
questions.prompt: A service calling Gemini 3.8 Flash through the Interactions API handles hundreds of thousands of requests daily. Its prompt order is currently [user-specific header, about 200 tokens] → [policy manual, about 3,000 tokens] → [fixed examples, about 1,200 tokens] → [question]. It wants lower input costs while **preserving the original manual**, **not shortening the prompt**, and **retaining the Interactions API**. What is the most appropriate action?

options.text: Move the user-specific header next to the question so shared content forms a continuous prefix, and monitor usage.total_cached_tokens for hits.
Create an explicit cache with cached_content, reference it from Interactions API requests, and manage retention and renewal before expiry.
Keep the prompt order unchanged, but collect calls using the same manual into hourly groups and send them together within the same window.
Summarize the manual and fixed examples to reduce total length, keeping the user-specific header first.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are retaining the Interactions API and preserving the original manual. Implicit caching on Gemini 3.6/3.8 Flash requires at least 4,096 input tokens. To improve hits, the documentation recommends placing large shared content first and sending similar prefixes within a short interval. The initial user-specific header made every prefix different; moving it later creates a continuous shared prefix exceeding the minimum.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It changes only order, not content. The tradeoffs are that personalization reaches the model later and implicit-cache hits remain unguaranteed.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; confusing similar features)**: Explicit caching is unsupported in the Interactions API and on Gemini 4 Argon and later.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; approach for another situation)**: Grouping requests in time can help, but cannot produce hits when prefixes differ by user.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Shortening violates the explicit prohibition. Reducing length below 4,096 would also make the input ineligible for caching.

**References**: [Gemini Context caching](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching) · [Gemini API cost and latency optimization](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/optimization)

questions.title: Improving Gemini implicit-cache hit rates
questions.prompt: A Gemini 3.8 Flash business-unit app already places a large shared document of at least 4,096 tokens first and user-specific values last. However, **thousands of requests with the same prefix arrive together at night, while only one or two arrive sporadically during the day**, and implicit-cache hit rates are low. Choose TWO improvements.

options.text: Add the user’s name and session information to a header at the beginning to improve personalization.
Collect daytime requests using the same prefix and send them within a short time window.
Distribute calls evenly throughout the day to increase intervals and eliminate bursts.
Collect usage.total_cached_tokens and compare hit ratios before and after the changes.
Switch to Gemini 4 Argon and create and attach a new explicit cached_content cache.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clues are that the shared document is already first and daytime requests are sporadic. The documentation recommends sending similar prefixes within a short interval and checking response usage.total_cached_tokens for hits. Since order is already correct, the remaining variables are request spacing and measurement.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: User-specific values at the beginning change the prefix and reduce hits.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It directly addresses daytime request spacing. The tradeoff is delaying some requests while a group accumulates.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Wider intervals work against cache hits.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It measures the effect quantitatively.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; confusing similar features)**: Explicit caching is unsupported on Gemini 4 Argon and later.

**References**: [Gemini Context caching](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/caching)

questions.title: Shared default max_tokens settings and rate limits across three providers
questions.prompt:
An enterprise gateway sets max_tokens to 8,192 by default for all OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini requests. Actual responses average 400 tokens, but only the OpenAI route encounters early 429 errors as three business units share one project’s limits. Constraints:

- One unit’s monthly reports must allow **up to 6,000 output tokens without truncation**.
- No unit may **monopolize the other units’ limits**.
- An OpenAI usage commitment requires **retaining the OpenAI route**.
- Gateway changes should remain **small and configuration-level**.

Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Keep the 8,192 default for all providers and have the gateway immediately resend the same request whenever a 429 occurs.
Reduce every provider’s default to 500, including monthly reports, to reduce both limit consumption and latency.
For OpenAI only, use request-type defaults (600 for ordinary requests, 6,000 for reports) and separate projects per business unit; leave the others unchanged.
Route OpenAI requests to Claude first to avoid the failing route, keeping OpenAI only as backup.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are 6,000-token outputs and preventing monopolization. OpenAI rate-limit accounting uses the larger of max_tokens and a character-based token estimate, and unsuccessful requests also count. An oversized default therefore consumes limits faster than actual usage suggests. The documentation recommends setting max_tokens close to expected response size. Claude output tokens per minute (OTPM) counts actual generated tokens, not max_tokens. Gemini limits apply per project, not per key. OpenAI limits apply at organization and project levels, so separate business-unit projects prevent units from consuming one another’s project allocations.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Failed requests count toward limits, so immediate retries worsen the problem. The documentation recommends exponential backoff.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It addresses limit consumption but truncates 6,000-token reports.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It meets all four constraints. The tradeoffs are operating request-type classification, separate projects, and provider-specific defaults.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It avoids 429s but moves away from consuming the OpenAI commitment, violating the retention requirement.

**References**: [OpenAI Rate limits](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/rate-limits) · [Claude Rate limits](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits) · [Gemini Rate limits](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits)

questions.title: Choosing which workloads should use Priority
questions.prompt: One OpenAI project runs **payment support (real-time, latency is paramount)**, **bulk embeddings for month-end settlement**, and **quarterly model evaluations**. Support latency is inconsistent, so the team wants Priority processing. Embeddings only need to meet the month-end deadline; evaluations need to finish within one day. The team wants **the lowest feasible total cost**. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Use no Priority processing and request only higher Standard limits to address latency.
Apply Priority only to payment support, keep embeddings on Standard, and run evaluations through Batch.
Put payment support and quarterly evaluations on Priority to finish evaluations quickly, and run embeddings through Batch.
Apply Priority only to payment support, and use Batch for both bulk embeddings and quarterly evaluations.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are latency first and the lowest feasible total cost. The documentation describes Priority as suitable for user-facing apps with steady traffic, not data processing, evaluations, or irregular traffic. Standard and Priority share the same model rate limits. Batch supports multiple endpoints, including `/v1/embeddings`, costs 50% less than synchronous APIs, uses a 24-hour completion window, and does not consume standard rate limits. The month-end and within-one-day deadlines can use this 24-hour window.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Higher limits do not ensure consistent response latency, so the support requirement remains unmet.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It meets latency needs but misses savings by paying Standard rates for embeddings with a flexible deadline.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Embeddings become cheaper, but evaluations that only need to finish within a day incur a premium. Evaluation traffic also consumes support limits, and bursts may cause some requests to fall back to Standard.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It pays a premium only for latency-sensitive work and sends both flexible-deadline workloads through a cheaper route with separate limits. The tradeoff is managing processing tiers by workload.

**References**: [OpenAI Priority processing](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/priority-processing) · [OpenAI Batch](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch)

questions.title: Combining billing options for an EU processing project
questions.prompt:
A service operating an EU data-region project through the OpenAI API wants all of the following:

- **Guaranteed capacity during peaks**
- Continued **EU regional processing** (MAM approval is complete)
- **Minimum regional-endpoint surcharges**
- **Lower costs for a large daily evaluation workload**

The team can negotiate with OpenAI enterprise sales. Which combination is most appropriate?

options.text: Purchase Reserved Tier capacity for all traffic, including evaluations, and use it for both peaks and nighttime evaluations.
Buy no Reserved Tier and send all peak calls through Priority for lower latency and processing precedence.
Abandon EU processing and move to a global endpoint to avoid the surcharge, leaving other settings unchanged.
Purchase regional-processing Reserved Tier only for the steady baseline, separate evaluations into Batch, and handle overages with pay-as-you-go billing.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are guaranteed peak capacity and lower evaluation costs. Reserved Tier is prepaid model-specific capacity and can apply to eligible regional-processing traffic, but it cannot be used for Batch or Flex, whose usage is billed pay-as-you-go. Usage above reserved capacity is also pay-as-you-go. Batch is 50% cheaper, and some models support EU regional processing. Applicable models incur a 10% surcharge at data-region endpoints, and EU access requires MAM or ZDR.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Evaluations cannot use Reserved capacity under this arrangement, wasting prepaid capacity and losing the Batch discount.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; confusing similar features)**: Priority is a latency-priority tier, not a prepaid capacity guarantee. It shares limits with Standard, and bursts can downgrade some traffic to Standard.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It avoids the surcharge but abandons EU processing.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It balances all four requirements. The tradeoffs are the risk of unused prepaid capacity and accepting the 10% surcharge.

This reflects documentation as of the reference date; Reserved Tier terms may vary through sales negotiations.

**References**: [OpenAI Reserved Tier](https://openai.com/api-reserved-tier/) · [OpenAI Your data](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/your-data) · [OpenAI Batch](https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/guides/batch)

questions.title: Frequent Standard downgrades after adopting Gemini API Priority
questions.prompt:
A business unit has just adopted Gemini API Priority, but some latency-sensitive requests are **frequently processed as Standard**. It faces these constraints:

- Priority costs **75–100% more than Standard**, making a higher monthly budget difficult.
- It must **continue protecting latency-sensitive service quality**.
- Internal batch and summarization calls also use Priority in the same project.
- Requested limit increases are **not guaranteed**.

Choose TWO correct diagnoses and actions.

options.text: Recognize that Priority limits are project-level and lower by default than Standard limits; request an increase, but keep Priority usage within current limits until approval.
Keep both latency-sensitive and batch workloads on Priority, request higher limits, and double the monthly budget to reduce downgrades.
Assume a limit increase will soon be approved and accelerate new-customer onboarding to increase Priority traffic now.
Keep only latency-sensitive calls on Priority, moving batch-like and internal summarization calls to Standard or Batch to free Priority capacity.
Disable Priority entirely, return to Standard, and address slower periods with on-screen waiting notices.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are the 75–100% premium and unguaranteed limit increases. Gemini API default Priority limits are 0.3 times the Standard limits for each model and tier, and apply per project rather than per key. Priority requests exceeding limits are downgraded to Standard instead of returning an error. Increases can be requested through the usual form but are not guaranteed.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It diagnoses the limit structure and combines an increase request with usage adjustment. The tradeoff is reduced Priority traffic until approval.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It may reduce downgrades, but increases are unguaranteed and doubling the budget violates the budget constraint.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Increasing traffic on the assumption of approval causes more downgrades if approval is delayed or denied. Service quality cannot be protected under an unguaranteed increase.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: It uses Priority only where the premium is justified and reduces cost. The tradeoff is managing routes by purpose.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It meets cost needs but abandons protection of latency-sensitive service quality.

This reflects documentation as of the reference date; Priority limit policies may change.

**References**: [Gemini API Rate limits](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/rate-limits) · [Gemini API cost and latency optimization](https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/optimization)

questions.title: Routing mixed EU and non-EU Claude traffic on Google Cloud
questions.prompt:
An enterprise calling Claude under a Google Cloud commitment spends about KRW 200 million monthly on pay-as-you-go usage. Approximately 30% comes from its German and French entities. Requirements:

- European-entity requests must **be processed only in the EU**.
- The other 70% has no location restriction.
- **Every request uses the latest model**.
- **Minimize regional surcharges**, while keeping as few routes as possible to reduce **operational burden**.

Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Send all requests to the eu multi-region endpoint, keeping one route and accepting the 10% surcharge on non-European traffic too.
Send everything to global to minimize both surcharges and routes, addressing European entities’ EU-processing requirements through contractual language.
Send European-entity requests to the eu multi-region endpoint and the rest to global, accepting two routes and a 10% surcharge on European traffic.
Use an older model supported on an EU regional endpoint for European requests and the latest model on global for the rest, accepting the older generation and a 10% surcharge for Europe.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are EU-only processing and minimum additional cost. Claude on Google Cloud documentation says global does not specify processing location, while regional and multi-region endpoints restrict processing to their locations at a 10% premium over global. An example note in the same documentation states that some regional endpoints support Sonnet 4.6 and earlier, while newer models require global or multi-region endpoints. Routing only EU-required traffic to a multi-region endpoint therefore limits the surcharge to 30% of usage while retaining the latest model. The tradeoffs are operating two routes and paying the 10% premium on European usage.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It uses one route but also charges the premium on the unrestricted 70%, violating minimum additional cost.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It minimizes costs and routes, but global does not restrict processing location. Contract language cannot replace EU processing.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It preserves EU processing, the latest model, and minimum surcharges while compromising on operational simplicity.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: EU processing is preserved, but European requests use an older model, violating the latest-model requirement for every request.

Regional model availability can change; check Model Garden before purchasing.

**References**: [Claude on Google Cloud › Endpoints and pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/build-with-claude/claude-on-vertex-ai) · [Data residency](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/manage-claude/data-residency)

questions.title: Configuring Batch for overnight classification restricted to US inference
questions.prompt:
Each night, Claude Sonnet 5.5 classifies about 250,000 customer inquiries; results are needed only within one day (24 hours). Every request begins with the same roughly 8,000-token classification instructions. Requirements:

- Because personal data is included, **inference runs only on US infrastructure**.
- Minimize cost.
- Haiku 5.5 failed the classification-accuracy threshold in evaluation, so **retain Sonnet 5.5**.
- The organization’s batch queue limit is 300,000 requests.

The first three requirements are mandatory, and delayed results are acceptable. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Use synchronous Messages API calls spread throughout the night with inference_geo set to "us" and a five-minute cache on the instruction prefix.
Submit three batches of about 84,000 requests each, leave inference_geo unspecified, and apply a one-hour cache to the instruction prefix.
Submit three batches of about 84,000 requests each, set inference_geo to "us" on every request, and apply a one-hour cache to the instruction prefix.
Downgrade to Haiku 5.5, submit three batches, set inference_geo to "us" on every request, and apply a one-hour cache to the instruction prefix.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are US-only inference and minimum cost. Claude Batch discounts both input and output tokens by 50%, and combines with prompt-cache discounts and data-region multipliers. Each batch allows up to 100,000 requests or 256MB, so 250,000 requests require at least three batches and fit the 300,000-request queue limit. Each batch request can have its own inference_geo. On Claude 4.6 and later, "us" applies a 1.1 multiplier to input, output, cache writes, and cache reads. Since batches may take longer than five minutes, documentation recommends considering a one-hour cache. One-hour writes cost 2 times the base input rate, and Sonnet 5.5 reads cost 0.05 times. The tradeoffs are the 1.1 multiplier on all tokens and the 2-times one-hour write cost. Most batches finish within an hour, but expire if incomplete after 24 hours, so tolerance for delay is necessary.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It preserves US inference but gives up the 50% Batch discount, violating minimum feasible cost. Batch suits the stated tolerance for delayed results.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Without a region, routing defaults to global and inference may occur outside the US. Avoiding the 1.1 premium violates US-only inference.

questions.prompt:
A business unit is migrating nightly document-embedding generation from synchronous calls to OpenAI Batch to **reduce costs without consuming daytime service rate limits**. - (1) Poll the created batch’s status and confirm completion.
- (2) Create a JSONL input file with a unique custom_id for each request.
- (3) Download the output, match it to requests by custom_id, and collect error-file entries for reprocessing.
- (4) Upload the input file through the Files API with purpose set to batch.

items.text: Poll the created batch’s status and confirm completion.
Create a JSONL input file with a unique custom_id for each request.
Download the output, match it to requests by custom_id, and collect error-file entries for reprocessing.
Upload the input file through the Files API with purpose set to batch.
Create a batch specifying the uploaded file ID, endpoint, and completion window.

questions.explanation:
The order follows dependencies: each step’s output becomes input to the next. The decisive requirements are exact request/result matching and retrying failures. OpenAI Batch documentation describes preparing JSONL, uploading through the Files API, creating a batch, checking status, and retrieving results.

| Order | Step | Dependency | Evidence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | (2) Prepare JSONL input | Starting point; custom_id enables later result matching. | Every line contains custom_id, method, url, and body, and one file targets only one model. |
| 2 | (4) Upload through Files API | Requires the file created in (2). | Set purpose to batch during upload. |
| 3 | (5) Create the batch | Uses the file ID returned in (4) as input_file_id. | Specify the input file ID, endpoint, and completion window. |
| 4 | (1) Check status | The batch created in (5) provides the object to query. | The output file is finalized when status is completed. |
| 5 | (3) Retrieve results and identify retries | Retrieve output_file_id and error_file_id files after (1) confirms completion. | Output order may differ from input order, so match by custom_id. |

questions.title: Controlling retention at different locations in Claude Code Enterprise
questions.prompt:
A company with offices in three countries uses Claude Code with Enterprise accounts. Security and audit needs conflict:

- Auditors require server-side usage records to remain for the **standard retention period**, so ZDR is not used.
- Security wants to minimize **plaintext session records on developer PCs**.

- Legal wants to block the path where conversations shared externally through `/feedback` are **retained long-term**.

Which combination is most appropriate?

options.text: Apply for ZDR to remove server-side records, reduce local retention to seven days, and set `DISABLE_FEEDBACK_COMMAND` to 1.
Keep standard server retention without ZDR, set `cleanupPeriodDays` to 7, and set `DISABLE_FEEDBACK_COMMAND` to 1.
Keep standard server retention without ZDR, reduce local retention to one day, and set `DISABLE_FEEDBACK_COMMAND` to 1.

The decisive constraints are standard server retention, resuming sessions within the past week, and minimizing plaintext local history. Local session history is stored in plaintext in `~/.claude/projects/` for 30 days by default, adjustable through `cleanupPeriodDays`. History shared through `/feedback` is retained for five years; `DISABLE_FEEDBACK_COMMAND=1` disables it.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Local and feedback requirements are met, but ZDR removes server records, conflicting with audit retention.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It satisfies all four requirements. The tradeoffs are inability to resume local sessions older than a week and inability to use server records for investigations beyond 30 days.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It minimizes plaintext history most, but sessions older than one day cannot be resumed locally, violating the one-week requirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Retention and resumption are appropriate, but feedback remains a five-year retention path, contrary to legal's requirement.

questions.title: Role-based control of improved memory in a healthcare workspace

Administrators should review who will receive access and notify those members of PHI restrictions before enabling it.

questions.title: Accepting feature loss when standardizing customer-managed keys

questions.title: Combining Fable 5.1 escalation and overnight processing in a ZDR organization

- Minimize overnight classification costs.
- The hardest 5% of cases require Fable 5.1-level quality. Send **only de-identified text** for those cases; 30-day retention is allowed.
- Stay within the existing organization without new organizations or contract changes.

Mandatory retention and quality requirements must be met; cost savings may be conceded. Which configuration is most appropriate?

options.text: Use Batch for overnight classification to halve cost and Messages for real-time calls. De-identify the hardest 5% and send them to Fable 5.1 in a 30-day-retention workspace.
Use Messages in a workspace retaining ZDR for real-time and overnight classification. De-identify the hardest 5% and process them with Fable 5.1 in another workspace with 30-day retention enabled.
Process every call through Messages with Opus 5.5 in the ZDR workspace, including the hardest 5% with the same model and workspace.
Use Messages in a ZDR workspace for real-time and overnight work, but send the hardest 5% as unmodified original text to Fable 5.1 in a 30-day-retention workspace.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are no retained original data and Fable 5.1 quality for the hardest 5%. Claude documentation states that Batch is ZDR-ineligible with 29-day retention. Covered Models such as Fable 5.1 and Mythos 5.1 require 30-day retention and cannot use ZDR without explicit Anthropic approval. A ZDR organization can enable 30-day retention in one workspace for these models. The Default Workspace always follows organization settings, so another workspace is needed. - **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It meets the mandatory requirements while conceding overnight cost savings.

questions.title: Re-estimating costs for 30 services migrating from Sonnet 4.6 to 5.5
questions.prompt:
Thirty Claude API services using Sonnet 4.6 will migrate to Sonnet 5.5. They fall into three categories: primarily text, primarily image inputs, and long outputs. Constraints:

- Post-migration quarterly spending **must not exceed 110% of current spending**.
- Every service must pass a **quality gate using a shared evaluation set**.
- The deadline is **six weeks away**, with three staff members.

What should come first in cost re-estimation and migration planning?

options.text: Add 30% for the extra tokens representing the same text, finalize the budget, change model IDs for all 30 services in one week, and replace service-level gates with first-month production metrics.

Group services into the three categories, remeasure token usage and thinking effects with representative traffic, set category caps using cost by effort level, and migrate services sequentially as they pass gates.
Remeasure full traffic samples and complete effort sweeps separately for all 30 services, then migrate passing services together at the week-six deadline.
Set every service to low effort to fit the budget, migrate first, and run quality gates afterward to fix failures.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are 110% of current spending, six weeks with three people, and quality gates. Sonnet 5.5 has lower per-token prices than 4.6, but the same text uses about 30% more tokens, thinking is enabled by default and can increase output tokens, and image tokens also increase. The migration guide recommends recounting tokens, sweeping effort, and rebaselining costs. Start with category-level measured usage and caps rather than a price table or blanket uplift, then migrate in gate-passing order. The tradeoffs are approximate category caps rather than exact per-service values and some migrations occurring near the deadline.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It accounts for token growth but collapses thinking and image effects into one uplift and replaces required gates with production metrics.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Category measurement makes budget caps feasible within staffing and time limits, while gate-based sequencing preserves quality.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Measurement is precise, but separate full measurements and sweeps for 30 services are difficult for three people within six weeks.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It reduces costs but postpones mandatory gates until after migration.

**References**: [Claude Sonnet 5.5 migration guide](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/sonnet-5-5/migration-guide) · [Pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing)

questions.title: Finding legacy settings that return 400 during a Sonnet 5.5 migration

options.text: Set `temperature=0.2` for an extraction request.
For a latency-sensitive service, set thinking to `{"type": "between_tools"}` and effort to low.
Force `tool_choice` to `{"type": "tool", "name": "classify"}` for classification.

The Sonnet 5.5 migration guide lists 400 errors for nondefault `temperature`, `top_p`, and `top_k`; `tool_choice` with type any or tool; thinking disabled and `budget_tokens`; and assistant prefill. Conversely, `between_tools` supports low, medium, and high effort; automatic tool choice with strict tools is a documented replacement for forced tool use; and the prompt-caching minimum falls to 512 tokens.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Nondefault temperature causes 400 and must be removed.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; appropriate for a different situation)**: This is a documented valid configuration for turning thinking off. It causes 400 only at xhigh or max effort.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: A forced tool choice causes 400; replace it with auto, strict tools, and instructions.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; appropriate for a different situation)**: This is the documented alternative.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; confuses related capabilities)**: Caching is not prohibited, and the lower 512-token minimum makes it easier to use.
