questions.title: Classifying 40 Haiku 4.5 services for caching and Batch during Sonnet 5.5 migration
questions.prompt:
Forty Claude API services using Haiku 4.5 will move to Sonnet 5.5. Requirements:

- Approximately 30 need **real-time responses** while users wait; the other ten produce overnight reports due the next morning.
- Total cost **must not exceed 140% of current cost**. Per million tokens, Haiku 4.5 costs $1 input/$5 output, and Sonnet 5.5 costs $2 input/$10 output.
- Many real-time services send a fixed policy-manual prefix of about 1,000–3,000 tokens with every request.
- Finish **within the migration quarter**, with limited staff.

Which migration design is most appropriate?

options.text: Use Message Batches for the ten overnight reports for a 50% discount. Migrate real-time services beginning with newly cacheable ones, leaving services on Haiku if the cap would be exceeded.
Move all 40 services to Sonnet 5.5 and Message Batches for a 50% discount, showing processing notices and making real-time users wait.
Move all 40 to Sonnet 5.5 with Haiku-era settings and no caching or Batch to minimize changes, settling costs at quarter-end.
Move the 30 real-time services to Sonnet 5.5 and append a new roughly 3,000-token shared prefix to each to improve cache hits, while processing overnight reports through real-time calls too.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are the 140% cost cap and real-time responses. Sonnet 5.5 has higher per-token prices than Haiku 4.5, uses about 30% more tokens for the same text, and enables thinking by default. However, its caching minimum falls from 4,096 to 512 tokens, making 1,000–3,000-token prefixes newly eligible; cache reads cost far less than input tokens. Message Batches provides a 50% discount but is asynchronous. Separate work that can wait into Batch and migrate real-time work by cache eligibility. The tradeoffs are leaving some services on Haiku and additional classification work.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Classification by service characteristics resolves conflicts among cost, real-time behavior, and schedule.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Costs fall, but asynchronous Batch violates the 30 services' real-time requirement.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Changes are small, but ignoring newly available caching and Batch makes exceeding the cost cap likely.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Real-time behavior is preserved, but adding prefixes is a substantial change and increases input tokens; foregoing Batch discounts for reports makes the cap difficult to meet.

**References**: [Claude Sonnet 5.5 migration guide › Migrating from Haiku 4.5](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/models/sonnet-5-5/migration-guide) · [Pricing](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/about-claude/pricing)

questions.title: Migration priorities under OpenAI retirement schedules and staffing limits

Model validation depends on Evals, making evaluation migration a prerequisite. These dates are the documentation's values as of 2026-10-16, not immutable guarantees. The tradeoff is postponing migration of the highest-traffic models.

questions.title: Migrating a fine-tuned gpt-4.1-mini model before retirement
questions.prompt:
Hansol Logistics' inquiry-classification service makes 1.2 million monthly calls to a model fine-tuned from gpt-4.1-mini. OpenAI documentation as of 2026-10-16 states that the GPT-4.1 mini snapshot retires on 2027-01-14, fine-tuned models follow their base model's schedule, and even existing customers cannot create new fine-tuning jobs from 2027-01-06. Internal constraints:

- Service must continue uninterrupted after 2027-01-14.
- A production-change freeze from December 15 through January 10 prohibits cutover during that period.
- Before cutover, compare old and new models **in parallel for four weeks** and verify classification F1 is at least the current level.
- Data-processing contracts cover only OpenAI; another provider requires three months of security review.

The first three constraints are mandatory. Which migration approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Move to gpt-6-luna with examples selected from existing training data in the prompt. Start four weeks of parallel F1 comparison in mid-November and cut over before December 14.

Perform one final gpt-4.1-mini fine-tuning run in November with recent classification data, compare in parallel for four weeks from mid-November, and cut over to that new fine-tune before December 14.
Start another provider's security review now, then run four weeks of parallel comparison with example-based prompting after approval before cutting over.
Keep the existing fine-tune until the freeze ends on January 11, switch to gpt-6-luna with examples, and check F1 for several days afterward.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are uninterrupted operation after 2027-01-14 and four weeks of parallel comparison before cutover. OpenAI recommends gpt-6-luna as the GPT-4.1 mini replacement and states that fine-tuned inference lasts only until base-model retirement. New jobs are blocked from 2027-01-06, so refinetuning does not provide a post-retirement path. Combining the freeze with four weeks of comparison means cutover must finish before December 14, requiring comparison to start in mid-November. The tradeoff is abandoning short prompts enabled by fine-tuning and increasing per-call input tokens and cost through examples.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: It meets all three mandatory constraints while accepting increased per-call token cost.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Pre-freeze cutover is possible, but the new fine-tune retires with the same base model, failing continuity after January 14.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Three months of review alone ends in mid-January, making four-week comparison and pre-freeze cutover impossible and exceeding retirement.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Cutover precedes retirement but lacks four weeks of prior parallel comparison.

questions.title: Different Gemini API retirement schedules and embedding migration impact
questions.prompt:
A division runs three Gemini API services. Retirement information in the reference-date documentation is:

- Voice guidance: Live/TTS preview models, displayed retirement date 2026-11-17, with replacements such as gemini-3.8-live.
- Document search: approximately 100 million indexed vectors from gemini-embedding-001, displayed retirement date 2028-05-14, replacement gemini-embedding-2.
- Text summarization: GA gemini-3.5-flash, retirement N/A, automatic routing.

Constraints are **two evaluation staff**, **this quarter's budget cap**, and **no voice-service interruption**. Select TWO priority actions consistent with the reference-date documentation.

options.text: Prioritize evaluating and migrating voice guidance to the gemini-3.8-live family before the earliest displayed date, 2026-11-17.
Because old and new embeddings cannot be compared in one index after changing models, estimate reindexing scale and parallel-operation cost now and include them in budgets and schedules.
Do nothing now because embedding retirement is in 2028; perform all reindexing at once in early 2028.
Index new documents with gemini-embedding-2 and search them alongside old vectors in the same index to eliminate reindexing cost.
Wait for notice of the exact retirement date before starting replacement evaluation, since displayed preview dates are only earliest possible dates.

questions.explanation:
The decisive constraints are two evaluators, uninterrupted voice service, and the quarterly budget cap. Gemini's retirement table gives the earliest date a model may be retired; exact dates are announced in advance. gemini-embedding-001 is replaced by gemini-embedding-2, whose embedding space is incompatible: vectors cannot be compared directly, and upgrading requires re-embedding all existing data. Therefore, evaluate the most imminent preview replacement first, while estimating expensive reindexing now despite its later date. The tradeoff is postponing embedding execution while both evaluators focus on voice.

- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Even a distant retirement creates substantial reindexing costs that must enter budget plans now.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It defers staffing work but omits reindexing from budget planning, risking the cap.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Apparent savings come from comparing incompatible vectors, undermining retrieval quality.
- **{{option:E}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It saves evaluation effort now, but late notice may leave insufficient time to preserve uninterrupted voice service.

Dates reflect the reference-date documentation and must be rechecked before planning.

Canary a subset of production traffic to the Agent Platform endpoint.

questions.title: Conversation-history storage for provider portability
questions.prompt:
A platform team chooses a conversation-history format for an internal agent alternating between OpenAI Responses API and Claude API. Requirements:

- **Allow switching between providers** for portability.
- **Preserve reasoning context** when continuing with the same provider to protect quality and cost.
- Avoid large increases in storage or conversion code.

OpenAI reasoning items must be sent back when store=false to continue using them. Claude thinking blocks identify their originating model and are removed when sent to a model that cannot read them. Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Store the OpenAI Responses item array as canonical history, including reasoning items, and adapt it to Claude format on every Claude call.
Store only roles, text, and tool results flattened into text; discard reasoning so identical history can be sent to any provider without conversion.
Store Claude content blocks as canonical history and convert thinking blocks to text when sending them to another provider to preserve reasoning flow.
Use a provider-neutral canonical format for roles, text, and tool calls/results. Keep reasoning items in separate provider/model-specific fields and send them back when continuing with that provider.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are portability and preserving reasoning context. Responses uses typed items, including reasoning; with store=false, returned reasoning items must be sent back unchanged. Claude thinking blocks record their originating model. When a model cannot read them, the API removes them while the request succeeds and those input tokens are unbilled, but the model may reason again, increasing cost and latency. A neutral canonical record with separate provider-specific reasoning meets both needs. The tradeoffs are adapter code and re-reasoning cost on the first turn after switching.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: A provider-specific canonical format reduces portability and increases conversion code.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Portability is maximized, but even same-provider continuation loses reasoning context, harming quality and cost.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It binds storage to Claude, and thinking text sent elsewhere does not have the original block's effect.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: The canonical format remains neutral while same-provider reasoning is preserved. Switching discards reasoning items, accepting first-turn re-reasoning cost.

Refine the rubric through a small number of detailed review rounds, provide examples at every score level and pass/fail criteria, and aggregate evaluator judgments through consensus voting. Check judge agreement with human labels.
Average scores after one round, exclude evaluators far from the mean, and use that as final without further rounds or rubric examples.
Discard human judgments that disagree with the LLM judge and use the judge's numerical scores and pass thresholds as authoritative.

The decisive issues are differing interpretations and reducing variation. - **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It provides rubric calibration, examples, passing criteria, and consensus aggregation.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Averaging and excluding without calibration rounds do not resolve different criteria.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It elevates the judge over humans, reversing the intended validation of judge bias against human labels.

questions.title: Pre-release validation and recovery for a tuned Gemini model replacement
questions.prompt:
A division wants to deploy a new version of its Agent Platform tuned Gemini model, registered in Model Registry, across enterprise services. Governance requires:

- Compare the candidate and current version **using the same criteria before deployment**.
- Check generated outputs for **toxicity, coherence, factuality, and safety**.
- **Automate evaluation because staff are limited**.
- Be able to **return to the last stable version** when problems arise.

Select TWO suitable pre-release validation and recovery measures.

options.text: Gate only on traditional ML accuracy, precision, recall, and F1, without separately checking generated-output toxicity or factuality.
Compare candidate and current versions using Experiments and model evaluation, checking toxicity, coherence, factuality, and safety before deployment.
Have evaluators read and judge every candidate output before deployment and document their decisions.
Immediately deploy the candidate to all users and consider restoring the previous version only after complaints accumulate.
Track model versions and metadata in Model Registry and use lineage to return to the last stable version when generation-quality or harmfulness alerts fire.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are common-criteria comparison and restoring the last stable version. Google Cloud's operational-excellence guidance recommends Experiments for comparing candidate and current models and model evaluation for toxicity, coherence, factuality, and safety. It also describes initiating rollback through Model Monitoring and generation-quality/harmfulness alerts and using Model Registry lineage to find the last stable version. Registry recovery applies here because the model was tuned and registered by the team. The tradeoff is initial work for comparison runs and metric alerts.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Traditional ML metrics are valid checks but do not cover generated-output toxicity or factuality.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Automated tools verify comparable criteria and generative metrics.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Thorough human review conflicts with the need for automation under limited staffing.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Full deployment without evaluation violates comparison before release.
- **{{option:E}} (Correct)**: Version lineage and alerts provide a recovery route to the last stable version.

items.text: Calculate refusal rates separately from response `stop_reason` or `stop_details`, rather than the HTTP-error dashboard.
Include refused requests in cost reports because bio-category refusals may incur input charges even before output begins.

questions.title: Nightly cross-provider regression evaluation and evidence retention
questions.prompt:
Hansol Retail's platform team runs nightly regression sets of about 40,000 cases per division for three divisions using OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini, then uses them as release gates. Requirements:

- Reduce evaluation cost to about half of synchronous calls; results are needed only within one day.
- Retain **original per-request results for 90 days** as audit evidence for gate decisions.
- Compare divisions with **the same rubric and decision code**.
- Minimize new infrastructure and operations for the platform team.

The first three requirements are mandatory; the last may be conceded. Which design is most appropriate?

options.text: Call all three synchronous APIs in parallel, retain results internally for 90 days, and score them with shared decision code.
Submit Batch jobs to all three providers, download result files to internal storage immediately on completion for 90-day retention, and score them with shared decision code.
Submit Batch jobs to all three providers but leave results there until an audit request arrives, then download them; use shared decision code.
Let divisions use Batch with their own rubrics and scoring and submit only summary scores to the platform team to reduce implementation burden.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are half-price evaluation and 90-day original per-request evidence. All three providers offer Batch at 50% of standard prices, but result retention is shorter than 90 days: Claude retains results for 29 days after creation, OpenAI automatically deletes output files 30 days after completion, and Gemini makes results downloadable for six weeks by default. All require moving results to internal storage. OpenAI permits one model per input file and up to 50,000 requests per batch, so each division's 40,000 requests fit in one file. The tradeoff is operating three batch integrations and internal storage.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Retention and shared scoring are met, but synchronous calls lack the half-price Batch discount.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It meets all mandatory requirements while conceding minimum implementation and operations.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: Cost and shared scoring are met, but provider retention of 29 days, 30 days, and six weeks leaves no originals after 90 days.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; violates a constraint)**: It lowers implementation burden but violates shared rubrics and code, while summary scores do not preserve original per-request results.

- Make release decisions across divisions using **the same criteria**.
- Stay within the post-replacement **cost cap**.
- Avoid **quality regression**.
- With limited gate staff and quarterly model replacements, use a **reusable procedure**.

Which gate is most appropriate?

options.text: Have divisions run their own datasets at self-selected effort levels and submit passing reports; governance checks only report format and signatures.
Gate by model ID alone, allowing service teams to choose effort freely after that model ID passes once.
Gate each model-ID/effort combination. On replacement, run default and neighboring effort levels against a shared dataset and compare cost and quality with common passing criteria.
On every replacement, broadly evaluate effort levels for each service using its own dataset and deploy the highest-quality combination.

The decisive requirements are common criteria, cost and quality constraints, and reusability. Model-selection documentation lists different defaults: high for Sonnet 5.5 and medium for Opus 5.5 and Haiku 5.5. - (1) Initiate rollback when an alert arrives.
- (2) Release the new version as a canary to a subset of users.
- (3) Build an evaluation dataset appropriate to the service's purpose.
- (4) Track quality and harmfulness metrics collected from canary traffic through evaluation, logging, and monitoring.

What is the correct order?

Release the new version as a canary to a subset of users.
Build an evaluation dataset appropriate to the service's purpose.
Track quality and harmfulness metrics collected from canary traffic through evaluation, logging, and monitoring.
Run predeployment evaluation using the dataset.

questions.title: Federating login with an internal identity provider and enforcing MFA centrally
questions.prompt:
Serim Insurance is launching an internal AI portal for 8,000 employees. Security requires:

- Employees sign in once with existing corporate accounts, without creating portal passwords.
- The portal neither stores nor validates employee passwords.
- Additional authentication factors (MFA) are enforced **in one place: the internal identity provider's (IdP) login policy**, not implemented separately in each portal.

The platform team plans SAML 2.0 federated identity. Which configuration is best?

options.text: Implement a portal user database with password and OTP validation, and require employees to register on first use.
Register the portal as a SAML service provider (SP) with the IdP. SAML federation automatically guarantees MFA, so leave IdP login policy unchanged and perform no further portal checks.
Register the portal as a SAML SP. Let the IdP authenticate employees and require MFA in its login policy. The portal validates the IdP-signed SAML assertion to allow login.
Periodically replicate IdP password hashes into the portal for direct password validation, and add separate portal OTP-based MFA.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [portal neither stores nor validates passwords] and [enforcement in one IdP login policy]. The SAML technical overview defines identity provider (IdP) and service provider (SP) roles for multi-domain SSO: the authenticating party creates an assertion describing authentication, and the relying party consumes it. Federated identity exists when partners agree how they refer to users. An authentication statement records how and when a user authenticated; an SP may request information about authentication method and strength. MFA proves two or more different factor types (knowledge, possession, inherence) in one authentication event. It depends on how the IdP authenticates users, not on SAML itself. Enable MFA in IdP policy and convey its result to the portal through SAML.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Storing/validating passwords and implementing separate MFA violates all three requirements: no separate password, no password storage, centralized MFA.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: SAML conveys authentication results but does not enforce MFA. If the IdP accepts a password alone, federation still provides no MFA.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: Authentication and MFA are centralized at the IdP; the portal validates signed assertions and handles login, meeting all three requirements.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Replicated password hashes make the portal validate passwords and create a second password store. Separate portal MFA also violates the requirements.

Additional note: For sensitive portal functions, the portal can inspect authentication-context information in assertions and request reauthentication at the IdP when strength is insufficient. Support varies by IdP and portal product; verify before adoption.

**Sources**: Standards — [SAML 2.0 Technical Overview (OASIS) §2.1, §3.1, §4.1, §4.3](https://docs.oasis-open.org/security/saml/Post2.0/sstc-saml-tech-overview-2.0.html) (verified wording: "SAML defines the roles called identity provider (IdP) and service provider (SP)", "The user is said to have a federated identity when partners have established such an agreement"; authentication statements record "the particular means used to authenticate the user") · [NIST SP 800-63B-4](https://pages.nist.gov/800-63-4/sp800-63b.html) (current edition; AAL2 requires "Proof of possession and control of two distinct authentication factors"; "A multi-factor authenticator requires two factors to execute a single authentication event". Earlier 800-63B-3 has been superseded).

questions.title: Document access through attribute rules: ABAC versus document ACLs
questions.prompt: Hanul Financial Group's shared search layer indexes about 1.2 million documents. Metadata records each document's owning division, security level (1–4), and permitted countries. The access rule is: “Return a document only when the user's division matches its division, the user's level is at least its level, and the user's work country is permitted.” HR maintains user attributes and processes **thousands of transfers and promotions monthly**. Rule changes, such as adjusting level thresholds, should not require reindexing 1.2 million documents. Which access-control approach is best?

options.text: Index only document attributes. At query time, obtain user attributes from HR, evaluate policy, and create search filters (ABAC). If an exceptional document is shared with one individual, add an individual allowlist only to that document.
Store a permitted-user ACL on every indexed document and update all relevant lists whenever an employee transfers.
Create a dedicated index for each user containing copies only of documents they can access.
Put all documents in one index and instruct the model in the system prompt not to use documents that mismatch the user’s division, level, or country.

questions.explanation:
The decisive details are [thousands of monthly personnel changes] and [no reindexing for policy changes]. NIST SP 800-162 describes ABAC as deciding authorization by evaluating attributes of subjects, objects, requested operations, and sometimes environmental conditions against policies or rules. The scenario's rule is already an attribute comparison of division, level, and country. Base decisions on attributes and policies rather than per-document lists. An ACL generally lists subjects permitted to access each object; frequent user-attribute changes require continual list updates.

- **{{option:A}} (Correct)**: Personnel changes update user attributes; rule changes update policy, avoiding reindexing. Use individual lists only for exceptional sharing that is difficult to express through attributes. The tradeoff is obtaining accurate user attributes at query time: HR data quality determines access-control quality.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; solution for another situation)**: Document ACLs suit individual sharing and exceptions on a small number of documents. Across 1.2 million documents and thousands of changes monthly, list maintenance is continuous, and rule changes require recomputing all lists.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: Per-user copies provide isolation but multiply storage/synchronization costs by user count and require moving copies on transfers.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Model instructions are not access control. Unauthorized documents have already been retrieved into model input and may be exposed through instruction violations or prompt injection. Apply filtering during retrieval.

Additional note: Existing Q05 and Q07 address synchronizing source-system ACL groups and division isolation boundaries. This conceptual question distinguishes list-based versus attribute-rule-based decisions; real systems often combine them.

**Sources**: Standard — [NIST SP 800-162 Guide to ABAC (abstract)](https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/162/upd2/final) (verified: decisions compare subject, object, requested-operation, and sometimes environmental attributes against policy/rules; the abstract does not compare ACLs) · General knowledge (ACLs as per-object permitted-subject lists; the comparison above is the question author's explanation).

questions.title: Distinguishing Deprecation and Sunset response headers
questions.prompt: Starting today (2026-10-19), v1 of Daewon Group's internal summary API—its own service, not a vendor API—returns two HTTP headers: `Deprecation` dated 2026-09-30 and `Sunset` dated 2027-03-31. v1 currently responds normally. The gateway operator wants 40 calling services to migrate to v2 **without service interruption**. What is the best response?

options.text: Because the `Deprecation` date has passed, assume v1 is unresponsive and issue an emergency notice requiring all 40 services to migrate this week.
The `Sunset` date is merely a hint; ignore it and migrate services only when actual errors begin.
The two headers convey the same information under different names; monitor only `Deprecation` and ignore `Sunset`.

Read `Deprecation` as “no longer recommended, but currently operational” and `Sunset` as the expected time of becoming unresponsive. Notify all 40 services to begin migration, set deadlines well before `Sunset`, and alert when these headers appear in responses.

questions.explanation:
The decisive details are [v1 currently responds normally] and [without interruption]. RFC 8594's Sunset header indicates that a URI is likely to become unresponsive at a future date. It is intended for the second phase of retirement—removal/nonresponsiveness—not the initial deprecation phase where a resource is no longer preferred but still works. Clients should treat its timestamp as a hint. RFC 9745's Deprecation header announces current or planned deprecation, but deprecation does not change resource behavior. A Sunset timestamp must not precede Deprecation.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: Deprecation is a notice that does not change behavior. Passing the date does not stop v1 responding or justify emergency migration.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: “Hint” means not guaranteed, not safe to ignore. Waiting for failures violates uninterrupted operation.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; confusing related features)**: The headers describe different phases. Deprecation alone gives no expected response-stop time for a migration deadline.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Distinguish the phases, start migration now, and set deadlines and alerts around the expected shutdown.

Additional note: This Sunset question concerns an HTTP header standard. Vendor-model retirement schedules are covered in Q16 and Q26. Vendor APIs are not guaranteed to emit these headers; track official retirement notices separately.

**Sources**: Standards — [RFC 8594 The Sunset HTTP Header Field](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8594.html) ("indicates that a URI is likely to become unresponsive at a specified point in the future"; clients treat Sunset time as a hint) · [RFC 9745 The Deprecation HTTP Response Header Field](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9745.html) ("The act of deprecation does not change any behavior of the resource"; "The timestamp given in the Sunset HTTP header field MUST NOT be earlier than the one given in the Deprecation header field").

questions.title: Data lineage versus audit trails in a quality-regression investigation
questions.prompt:
Since last week, Nuri Life's customer-service assistant has quoted incorrect surrender-value amounts. The quality team needs to determine:

- (a) **Which source document and version**, and **which processing stages** such as chunking, embedding, and filtering, produced the indexed evidence paragraph cited by the wrong answer.
- (b) **Who changed which index settings and prompt templates, and when**, last week.

Which records are correctly matched to these needs?

options.text: (a) Audit Trail; (b) Data Lineage
(a) Data Lineage; (b) Audit Trail
Both (a) and (b): a quality-score dashboard showing weekly evaluation trends
Both (a) and (b): a data-lineage tool alone is sufficient; audit trails are needed only for legal requirements

questions.explanation:
The decisive phrases are (a) [which source version and processing stages] and (b) [who changed which settings and when]. Google Cloud describes data lineage as a map of the data lifecycle showing origins, destinations, and transformations, used for troubleshooting, impact analysis, auditing, and compliance. NIST defines an audit trail as a chronological record of system activities sufficient to reconstruct activities; it generally records who did what and when. (a) concerns data flow and transformations; (b) concerns human actions.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; confusing related features)**: The targets are reversed. Audit trails are not designed to show data-processing paths, and lineage is not an actor-action log.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: Lineage shows source-to-index paths and transformations; audit trails record actors and times for configuration changes.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; solution for another situation)**: Score trends monitor when quality declined, not the responsible document path or change actor.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: Lineage tracks origins and transformations, not change actors. Audit trails support change investigations even without legal requirements.

Additional note: Join both records using shared identifiers such as document version, index-build ID, and prompt version to trace which answers a change affected. See Q65 for selecting retrospective audit controls.

**Sources**: Official vendor explanation of general concepts — [Google Cloud › About data lineage](https://docs.cloud.google.com/knowledge-catalog/docs/about-data-lineage) ("a visual map that tracks the entire lifecycle of your data"; origins, destinations, transformations; impact analysis, troubleshooting, auditing) · Standard — [NIST CSRC Glossary › audit trail](https://csrc.nist.gov/glossary/term/audit_trail) ("A chronological record of system activities that is sufficient to enable the reconstruction" — NISTIR 7316 definition).

questions.title: How BYOK changes responsibilities on AWS
questions.prompt:
Hanul Financial's security team wants direct control over encryption keys for stored AI-platform data on AWS, including embedding indexes and logs. Requirements:

- Generate original key material in its own HSM and import a copy into AWS KMS (BYOK).
- Leave data-center and hypervisor physical/infrastructure security to AWS.
- Hanul remains responsible for key backups and access policies.

The team disagrees about responsibilities. Which explanation of the Shared Responsibility Model and BYOK is most accurate?

options.text: With BYOK, AWS assumes responsibility for both keys and data centers, so key-material backups can also be left to AWS.
Customer responsibilities are identical across all services, so customers are responsible for physical data-center security regardless of BYOK.

AWS protects cloud infrastructure; customers manage configuration, data, and keys within their selected services. With imported key material, customers remain responsible for its custody and durability, including originals and backups, and must securely retain the original separately.
Because BYOK lets AWS use a key copy, treat it as insufficient control and separately encrypt all data with an in-house module before uploading to AWS services.

questions.explanation:
The decisive requirements are [AWS handles data centers and hypervisors] and [Hanul handles key backups and access policies]. AWS's shared responsibility model assigns AWS protection of infrastructure running all AWS Cloud services, while customer responsibility depends on selected services. AWS KMS documentation calls importing key material BYOK: customers remain responsible for the material while allowing KMS to use a copy. Keeping originals outside AWS for durability and disaster recovery is the customer's responsibility.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: Responsibility for imported material remains with the customer. AWS does not recover it if the customer loses it.
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; factual error)**: Customer duties vary by service; physical security belongs to AWS infrastructure protection.
- **{{option:C}} (Correct)**: It correctly divides infrastructure protection from customer configuration/data/key management and identifies customer custody of BYOK originals.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: Generating and controlling original key material is satisfied by BYOK. Separately encrypting everything outside AWS complicates search and managed processing and increases operational burden.

Additional note: Deleted imported key material can be reimported to restore use, unlike deletion of an ordinary KMS key, which is irreversible after the waiting period. See Q74 for service-specific customer-managed-key support and functionality tradeoffs.

**Sources**: Official — [AWS Shared Responsibility Model](https://aws.amazon.com/compliance/shared-responsibility-model/) ("AWS is responsible for protecting the infrastructure that runs all of the services offered in the AWS Cloud"; "Customer responsibility will be determined by the AWS Cloud services that a customer selects") · [AWS KMS › Importing key material](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/kms/latest/developerguide/importing-keys.html) ("a feature often known as 'bring your own key' (BYOK)"; "you remain responsible for the key material while allowing AWS KMS to use a copy of it").

questions.title: Which design meets requirement 1?
questions.prompt: Which design meets requirement 1?
questions.context:
[Company overview] Daewon Group has three subsidiaries: Daewon Precision, Daewon Motors, and Daewon Energy. Its AI platform team operates one internal document-summary API behind a single gateway, called by all three subsidiaries.

[Existing environment] The API uses one vendor's model. **Contract and security-review requirements permit only one vendor organization and API key**; no new keys or organizations may be issued. All subsidiaries share one processing pool. Yesterday, a surge in Daewon Motors' nightly batch visibly slowed Daewon Energy's responses. Monthly vendor bills have been allocated by subsidiary headcount.

[Requirement 1] A surge in one subsidiary must not slow others. Keep one platform without separate subsidiary stacks (gateway, retrieval layer, serving environment). Allocate costs by **actual usage**, recorded accurately per request for month-end settlement. FinOps holds monthly subsidiary usage reviews.

[Requirement 2] The team wants to upgrade the summary API's underlying model. (1) No subsidiary user may receive new-model responses before validation finishes. (2) After validation, route only a small portion of real traffic to the new model, expand gradually while observing metrics, and immediately revert if metrics deteriorate. (3) Daewon Energy must contractually stay on the old model until its own validation finishes next quarter; pin only that subsidiary to the old version **without changing deployed code**.

options.text: Build a dedicated silo stack for each subsidiary with separate gateway, retrieval layer, and serving environment, and issue each its own vendor key.

Keep the shared pool. Extract the subsidiary/tenant identifier from authentication tokens at the gateway and attach it to each request. Enforce per-tenant request/token limits. Accurately store subsidiary ID, model, and input/output token counts for every request (metering), multiply usage by rates at month-end to allocate costs, and use those figures in FinOps reviews.
Keep an unlimited shared pool and headcount-based allocation, but have FinOps caution heavy users at monthly reviews.
Keep the shared pool and allocate costs using subsidiary call counts from sampled APM traces, without limits.

questions.explanation:
The decisive details are [Requirement 1: no dedicated stacks, actual usage, accurate per-request records] and [Existing environment: only one key]. In multi-tenancy, AWS SaaS Lens calls shared resources a pool and per-tenant dedicated resources a silo. Azure calls one tenant degrading another's performance a noisy neighbor, recommending resource governance such as throttling, rate limits, and per-tenant quotas. Azure's multitenancy guide also says consumption must be measured per tenant because most services do not automatically distinguish tenants, and billing/metering requires accurate storage that does not discard data through sampling. FinOps Foundation defines allocation as apportioning costs to the parties responsible for components. Metering (how much was consumed) is needed for allocation (whose cost it is).

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Strong isolation violates both no-dedicated-stacks and single-key constraints.
- **{{option:B}} (Correct)**: It keeps the pool while adding tenant identification, tenant limits to suppress noisy neighbors, per-request metering, and usage-based allocation. The tradeoff is operating the gateway and metering store.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Headcount is not actual usage; without limits, surges continue slowing other subsidiaries.
- **{{option:D}} (Incorrect; confusing related features)**: Observability tools often sample for performance analysis, so they cannot provide exact request-level settlement records. Metering and monitoring serve different purposes. No limits also violates isolation.

Additional note: Q10 and Q11 address allocation using vendor-console workspaces or projects. This question concerns platform-layer metering/allocation with a single vendor key. Check vendor documentation separately before using response token-usage fields as the authoritative metering source.

**Sources**: Official — [AWS Well-Architected SaaS Lens › Silo, pool, and bridge models](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/saas-lens/silo-pool-and-bridge-models.html) (silo: "tenants are provided dedicated resources"; pool: "tenants share resources") · [Azure Architecture Center › Noisy Neighbor antipattern](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/antipatterns/noisy-neighbor/noisy-neighbor) ("one tenant's performance is degraded because of the activities of another tenant"; "Apply resource governance") · [Azure Architecture Center › Measure the consumption of each tenant](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/azure/architecture/guide/multitenant/considerations/measure-consumption) ("it's important to measure the consumption of each tenant"; "For billing and metering purposes, choose a data store that gives you a high level of accuracy") · [FinOps Foundation › Allocation](https://www.finops.org/framework/capabilities/allocation/) ("Allocation defines how costs should be apportioned to those responsible for each component of that cost").

questions.title: Which model-transition process meets requirement 2?
questions.prompt: Which model-transition process meets requirement 2?
questions.context:
[Company overview] Daewon Group has three subsidiaries: Daewon Precision, Daewon Motors, and Daewon Energy. Its AI platform team operates one internal document-summary API behind a single gateway, called by all three subsidiaries.

[Existing environment] The API uses one vendor's model. **Contract and security-review requirements permit only one vendor organization and API key**; no new keys or organizations may be issued. All subsidiaries share one processing pool. Yesterday, a surge in Daewon Motors' nightly batch visibly slowed Daewon Energy's responses. Monthly vendor bills have been allocated by subsidiary headcount.

[Requirement 1] A surge in one subsidiary must not slow others. Keep one platform without separate subsidiary stacks (gateway, retrieval layer, serving environment). Allocate costs by **actual usage**, recorded accurately per request for month-end settlement. FinOps holds monthly subsidiary usage reviews.

[Requirement 2] The team wants to upgrade the summary API's underlying model. (1) No subsidiary user may receive new-model responses before validation finishes. (2) After validation, route only a small portion of real traffic to the new model, expand gradually while observing metrics, and immediately revert if metrics deteriorate. (3) Daewon Energy must contractually stay on the old model until its own validation finishes next quarter; pin only that subsidiary to the old version **without changing deployed code**.

options.text: Start validation with a canary sending 5% of all traffic to the new model, and migrate Daewon Energy the same way.

Shadow production requests to the new model without returning its responses to users, recording them for comparison. After validation, switch every subsidiary at once on the same day, reverting if problems appear.
Use shadow validation and a gradually expanded canary, but create a separate deployment pipeline and serving environment to keep Daewon Energy on the old version.

First, shadow copies of production requests to the new model, logging responses for comparison without exposing them to users. Second, canary a small share of real traffic, expand gradually, and automatically roll back on bad alarm metrics. Pin Daewon Energy to the old model through a per-subsidiary feature flag.

questions.explanation:
The decisive clauses in [Requirement 2] are (1) no user exposure before validation, (2) a small share of real traffic and immediate rollback, and (3) no deployment-code changes. SageMaker describes shadow testing as sending real-time production-request copies to a new variant while returning only production-variant responses to the application. Shadow responses may be discarded or logged for offline comparison. Its canary traffic shifting sends a portion of traffic to a new fleet, observes alarms during a baking period, and automatically rolls back on alarms. The distinction is user exposure: shadow responses do not reach users; canary responses do. Feature flags generally control feature exposure through configuration without redeploying code.

- **{{option:A}} (Incorrect; confusing related features)**: A 5% canary sends responses to real users, violating (1) before validation. It also fails Daewon Energy's pinning requirement (3).
- **{{option:B}} (Incorrect; constraint violation)**: Shadow is appropriate, but an all-at-once switch violates gradual rollout (2); all users encounter issues before rollback.
- **{{option:C}} (Incorrect; overengineering)**: The stages are correct, but separate deployment and serving infrastructure conflicts with requirement 1's no-dedicated-stack rule and (3)'s no-code-change intent. It adds operational burden where configuration suffices.
- **{{option:D}} (Correct)**: Shadow handles non-user-facing validation; canary handles gradual real traffic and automatic rollback; flags handle subsidiary-level pinning.

Additional note: Shadow adds model-call cost for mirrored requests and cannot measure user reactions because users never receive shadow responses. See Q16 and Q82 for evaluation gates and staged rollout in a full model-migration plan.

**Sources**: Official vendor explanations of general concepts — [Amazon SageMaker › Shadow tests](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/shadow-tests.html) ("Only the responses of the production variant are returned to the calling application"; "You can choose to discard or log the responses of the shadow variant for offline comparison") · [Amazon SageMaker › Blue/green deployments, canary traffic shifting](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/deployment-guardrails-blue-green-canary.html) ("you can test a portion of your endpoint traffic on the new fleet while the old fleet serves the remainder"; "If any of the alarms trip during the baking period, then SageMaker AI initiates a rollback") · General knowledge (Feature Flag: configuration-based exposure control; this term was not verified against official documentation).

questions.title: Beyond-seat usage with individual spending caps
questions.sourceTopic: Claude Enterprise · Cost controls
questions.prompt: In a seat-based Claude for Enterprise organization, members should be able to use Claude Code beyond their seat allowance, but each member must have an individual spending cap. Which combination is required?

options.text: Enable usage credits and set individual member spending limits.
Enable usage credits without setting spending limits.
Enable usage credits and set workspace spending limits.
Set modelPricing to contract prices and set individual member spending limits.
Create a Claude Code Analytics API key and enable usage credits.

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** Correct. Usage credits cover consumption beyond the seat allowance, and spending limits can be set at organization, group, or individual-member level.

- **{{option:B}}.** Without spending limits there is no individual cap, violating the requirement.

- **{{option:C}}.** Workspace spending limits are controls for API/Console organizations. Seat-based organization controls are in the claude.ai admin console.

- **{{option:D}}.** modelPricing changes only the unit prices used for reported costs. It does not enable usage beyond the allowance.

- **{{option:E}}.** The Claude Code Analytics API retrieves usage metrics and cannot set spending limits. It is also an API for Console organizations.

questions.title: Why one developer does not receive policy
questions.sourceTopic: Claude Code managed policies · Server delivery
questions.prompt: The organization distributes Claude Code policies through claude.ai administration, and they apply to most developers. One developer is signed in with the organization's claude.ai account and does not use apiKeyHelper, yet claude doctor's 'Managed settings (remote)' line reports that fetching was skipped. Which shell-profile entry, added for the internal LLM gateway, causes this?

options.text: The corporate proxy address in HTTPS_PROXY
The corporate CA bundle in NODE_EXTRA_CA_CERTS
A nondefault ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC=1
A gateway model alias in ANTHROPIC_MODEL

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** Shell proxy settings also apply to policy-fetch requests. They do not cause fetching to be skipped.

- **{{option:B}}.** This configures TLS certificate authorities and is not listed as a reason for skipping policy retrieval.

- **{{option:C}}.** Correct. Claude Code skips server-managed settings retrieval when the shell contains a nondefault ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL or a CLAUDE_CODE_USE_* provider variable.

- **{{option:D}}.** This disables nonessential traffic; the documentation does not identify it as a reason for skipping policy fetching.

- **{{option:E}}.** This chooses the model to use; it does not cause policy retrieval to be skipped.

questions.title: Authentication fails despite an active subscription
questions.sourceTopic: Claude Code authentication · Credential precedence
questions.prompt: A developer with an active subscription receives an organization-status authentication error from Claude Code. Their shell still contains a Console key for an inactive organization, and they approved using that key when first launching interactively. Which entry caused this key to be used instead of the subscription?

options.text: ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN
apiKeyHelper
CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN
ANTHROPIC_PROFILE
ANTHROPIC_API_KEY

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** This is a gateway token sent in the Authorization Bearer header. The documentation does not identify it as the Console key in that approval prompt.

- **{{option:B}}.** This is a setting whose script returns a key, not an environment variable. The question specifies a key left in an environment variable.

- **{{option:C}}.** This is a long-lived OAuth token for a subscription account, unrelated to an inactive organization's Console key.

- **{{option:D}}.** This variable selects a named profile. It is not a key and has no approval prompt asking whether to use it.

- **{{option:E}}.** Correct. Once approved, a Console key in this environment variable takes precedence over subscription login. A key belonging to an inactive organization can cause authentication failure.

questions.title: Combining plugin source, installation, and bypass controls
questions.sourceTopic: Claude Code managed policies · Plugins
questions.prompt: Managed policy must (1) restrict user plugin sources to the official marketplace and repositories in the internal GitHub organization, (2) install and enable two internal-marketplace plugins on every device, (3) block command-line loading of local-directory plugins for a single session, and (4) continue loading the team's directory-based plugins under ~/.claude/skills. Which configuration meets all four requirements?

options.text: Only strictKnownMarketplaces listing the official marketplace and internal GitHub organization repositories
strictKnownMarketplaces (official, internal GitHub organization, skills-dir) + extraKnownMarketplaces + enabledPlugins + disableSideloadFlags
blockedMarketplaces blocking external sources but not skills-dir + extraKnownMarketplaces + enabledPlugins + disableSideloadFlags
strictKnownMarketplaces (official, internal GitHub organization, skills-dir) + extraKnownMarketplaces + enabledPlugins, without command-line flag rejection
strictKnownMarketplaces (official and internal GitHub organization, without skills-dir) + extraKnownMarketplaces + enabledPlugins + disableSideloadFlags

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** An allowlist neither registers marketplaces nor installs plugins, and does not block --plugin-dir. It fails (2) and (3) and also lacks the skills-dir entry needed for (4).

- **{{option:B}}.** Correct. The allowlist satisfies (1), marketplace registration and enabledPlugins satisfy (2), rejection of sideload flags satisfies (3), and the skills-dir entry satisfies (4).

- **{{option:C}}.** A blocklist blocks only named sources. It cannot restrict all sources to the official and internal sources required by (1).

- **{{option:D}}.** Without command-line flag rejection, --plugin-dir remains a bypass for loading local plugins, violating (3).

- **{{option:E}}.** Without skills-dir in the allowlist, directory-based skills plugins do not load, violating (4).

questions.title: Connectors disappear after a fixed server list is deployed
questions.sourceTopic: Claude Code managed policies · MCP controls
questions.prompt: After a company deploys a fixed MCP server-list file to each device's system path, all claude.ai connectors disappear from terminal Claude Code, including connectors configured by organization administrators. Requirements are to (1) retain the fixed list's exclusive control, (2) prevent developers from re-enabling connectors through personal settings, and (3) keep the Slack connector blocked. Which diagnosis and action are correct?

options.text: An empty allowlist prevents loading. Add connector URL entries to allowedMcpServers.
The fixed server-list file causes it. Remove the file and switch to allowedMcpServers with allowManagedMcpServersOnly.
The fixed server-list file suppresses connectors. Have each developer set allowAllClaudeAiMcps to true in user settings.
The fixed server-list file suppresses connectors. Set allowAllClaudeAiMcps to true in an administrator-controlled policy source and block Slack with deniedMcpServers.
The fixed server-list file suppresses connectors. Set only allowAllClaudeAiMcps to true in an administrator-controlled policy source, without a denylist.

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** The allowlist does not apply to servers in the fixed-list file. The file's suppression of connectors is the actual cause, so this diagnosis is wrong.

- **{{option:B}}.** Removing the file loses the exclusive control required by (1).

- **{{option:C}}.** This key is read only from administrator-controlled layers such as server-managed settings, MDM, or system managed-settings files. User settings have no effect and will not restore connectors.

- **{{option:D}}.** Correct. The file suppresses connectors. allowAllClaudeAiMcps in an administrator-controlled layer loads connectors alongside the file, and allow/deny lists also apply to connectors, so deniedMcpServers can block Slack.

- **{{option:E}}.** Connectors return, but without a denylist entry Slack loads too, violating (3).

questions.title: The authorization path for daily developer metrics
questions.sourceTopic: Console organization · Usage metrics API and admin keys
questions.prompt: An administrator in a non-Enterprise, API-billed Console organization has the organization developer role and is a workspace admin for the Claude Code workspace. They want to retrieve daily per-developer Claude Code usage metrics programmatically. What is the correct path?

options.text: Ask a member with the organization admin role to create an admin API key.
Create an admin API key directly using their developer role.
Ask the organization owner to create an analytics-only key with read:analytics scope.
Create a workspace API key in the Claude Code workspace and use it.
Ask a member with the organization billing role to create an admin API key.

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** Correct. This metrics API requires an admin key, which only members with the organization admin role can create.

- **{{option:B}}.** The developer role can manage API keys but cannot create admin keys. In Console organizations, admin keys require the admin role.

- **{{option:C}}.** An analytics-only key with read:analytics scope is the Enterprise-organization path. This organization is not Enterprise.

- **{{option:D}}.** Keys cannot be manually created in the Claude Code workspace, and workspace keys do not work on admin endpoints.

- **{{option:E}}.** The billing role manages billing information. The admin role is required to create admin keys.

questions.title: Where to enforce organization-only access from first login
questions.sourceTopic: Claude Code authentication · Managed policy delivery
questions.prompt: A company already distributes organization-wide policy keys through claude.ai administration (server-managed settings) and will retain this arrangement. From a new employee's very first Claude Code login and thereafter, it must require claude.ai login and accounts belonging to its organization ID, without allowing users to change those values. Where should the login-method and permitted-organization-ID keys be placed?

options.text: Only in server-managed settings.
Only in device management, such as MDM or system managed-settings files.
In both device management and server-managed settings, with identical values.
In instructions to distribute a user settings file (~/.claude/settings.json).
In the repository's .claude/settings.json.

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** Server-managed settings reach only accounts already authenticated to the organization, so they cannot control the first login.

- **{{option:B}}.** Because server-managed settings remain in use, they become the selected source for policy keys after login and are not merged with device values. These keys are not documented exceptions, so device-only values lose effect after login.

- **{{option:C}}.** Correct. Device management applies the keys before first login. In an organization delivering policy keys through server-managed settings, sources are not merged, so the same keys must be present in both.

- **{{option:D}}.** Users can directly edit this file, violating the requirement that they cannot change the values.

- **{{option:E}}.** Repository settings are below managed policy and user-editable, so they cannot enforce this requirement.

questions.title: Server-enforced model controls with limited reach
questions.sourceTopic: Claude Code managed policies · Model controls
questions.prompt: Which model control is enforced on the server, disables individual unapproved models, and applies only to sessions authenticated through claude.ai or the Anthropic API, not Bedrock sessions?
questions.context:
**Environment:** Claude for Enterprise · Claude Code (a claude.ai-login team and an Amazon Bedrock team)

**Scenario:** A company uses Claude for Enterprise. Most developers sign in to Claude Code with claude.ai accounts, while some teams connect only through Amazon Bedrock and receive policy files through MDM. Security wants only approved models, the cost team wants effort caps, and the platform team wants to block outdated clients. Server-side enforcement is preferred where possible, but both connection paths must receive the same effect. The currently deployed managed policy is shown below.

```json
{
  "model": "sonnet",
  "minimumVersion": "2.1.250"
}
```

options.text: availableModels, a managed-settings key filtering the selector list
Organization model restrictions
Organization default model
deniedModels, a managed-settings key blocking specific versions
enforceAvailableModels, a managed-settings key restricting default options too

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** This managed-settings key applies through device policy regardless of provider. It does not meet the server-enforcement and no-Bedrock-reach conditions.

- **{{option:B}}.** Correct. Individual models are disabled in claude.ai admin settings and enforced server-side. This does not reach sessions using providers such as Bedrock.

- **{{option:C}}.** This sets the model with which a new session starts. It does not disable individual models.

- **{{option:D}}.** This managed-settings key blocks specific versions as a client-side policy. It does not meet the server-enforcement or no-Bedrock-reach conditions.

- **{{option:E}}.** This managed-settings key restricts default options to the allowed model list. It differs from individual model disabling and server-side enforcement.

questions.title: Keys that allow only approved model choices
questions.sourceTopic: Claude Code managed policies · Model controls
questions.prompt: Devices on the Bedrock team receive policy through MDM and must also allow only approved models, including preventing an unapproved model from appearing as a default selector option. What must be added to the supplied policy?
questions.context:
**Environment:** Claude for Enterprise · Claude Code (a claude.ai-login team and an Amazon Bedrock team)

**Scenario:** A company uses Claude for Enterprise. Most developers sign in to Claude Code with claude.ai accounts, while some teams connect only through Amazon Bedrock and receive policy files through MDM. Security wants only approved models, the cost team wants effort caps, and the platform team wants to block outdated clients. Server-side enforcement is preferred where possible, but both connection paths must receive the same effect. The currently deployed managed policy is shown below.

```json
{
  "model": "sonnet",
  "minimumVersion": "2.1.250"
}
```

options.text: Expand organization model restrictions and set managed model to an approved model.
Set availableModels together with model (an approved model).
Set only availableModels, without another key.
Set availableModels together with enforceAvailableModels.
Block specific versions with deniedModels and also set enforceAvailableModels.

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** Organization model restrictions do not reach Bedrock sessions. The managed model setting is only a startup default, not a lock.

- **{{option:B}}.** model is only a startup default, not a lock. A separate key is needed to constrain default options to the allowlist.

- **{{option:C}}.** This establishes an allowed model list but does not prevent a default option from resolving to a model outside it.

- **{{option:D}}.** Correct. The allowlist restricts the selector, and the additional key extends the restriction to default options and automatically selected default models. As managed settings, they also apply to the Bedrock team.

- **{{option:E}}.** A denylist blocks only specific versions and cannot meet the allowlist requirement of 'approved models only'.

questions.title: Why an older version still starts despite a minimum
questions.sourceTopic: Claude Code managed policies · Version controls
questions.prompt: After the supplied policy is deployed, a developer can still start and use Claude Code 2.1.200, below the minimum. The device receives only one server-managed settings source; claude doctor reports the deployed settings were loaded, and the developer has restarted afterward. What is the cause?
questions.context:
**Environment:** Claude for Enterprise · Claude Code (a claude.ai-login team and an Amazon Bedrock team)

**Scenario:** A company uses Claude for Enterprise. Most developers sign in to Claude Code with claude.ai accounts, while some teams connect only through Amazon Bedrock and receive policy files through MDM. Security wants only approved models, the cost team wants effort caps, and the platform team wants to block outdated clients. Server-side enforcement is preferred where possible, but both connection paths must receive the same effect. The currently deployed managed policy is shown below.

```json
{
  "model": "sonnet",
  "minimumVersion": "2.1.250"
}
```

options.text: forceRemoteSettingsRefresh is not enabled, so startup used cached policy instead of fetching it.
Multiple managed sources caused the default managedSourcesBehavior to ignore minimumVersion.
The developer's ~/.claude/settings.json overwrote minimumVersion with a lower value.
minimumVersion, like model, applies only on the next launch and the developer has not restarted.
The policy lacks requiredMinimumVersion; minimumVersion only prevents installation of versions below the floor.

questions.explanation:
- **{{option:A}}.** claude doctor reports loading the deployed settings, so this was not startup with a cached policy.

- **{{option:B}}.** The device receives only one managed source, leaving no source-selection conflict that could ignore the value.

- **{{option:C}}.** Managed settings take precedence over user settings, so a user file cannot overwrite the managed value.

- **{{option:D}}.** The developer already restarted. Moreover, the documentation lists model and other keys as next-launch settings, not minimumVersion.

- **{{option:E}}.** Correct. minimumVersion only prevents updates from installing below the floor. The requiredMinimumVersion family rejects startup of out-of-range versions.

questions.sourceTopic: Claude Code authentication · Managed policies

guide:
### 1. Introduction

**Purpose**: This exam assesses whether candidates can design enterprise AI platforms spanning organizations, models, and vendors, and evaluate tradeoffs among regulatory, cost, and lifecycle requirements.

**Objectives**

- Design enterprise AI architectures for current and anticipated business requirements.
- Determine the right combination of enterprise applications and custom API-based development.
- Design shared platforms with gateways, shared retrieval layers, and permission propagation.
- Optimize large-scale traffic cost and capacity through combinations of billing options.
- Design multinational compliance controls combining enterprise-app security, zero retention, regional processing, audit logs, and filtering layers.
- Establish portability and migration strategies for model retirement and vendor replacement.
- Standardize release criteria across business units using shared evaluations and production quality monitoring.

### 2. Target Candidates

- AI architects, enterprise architects, AI platform architects, technical leads

**Recommended background and exam scope**

- At least two years of AI architecture experience and SDA-level knowledge are recommended.
- Code-level implementation of individual agents is outside scope (covered by AEP).

### 3. Content Domains

| Domain | Weight |
| --- | --- |
| 1. Organizational Requirements and Adoption Strategy | 15% |
| 2. Enterprise Platform Architecture | 22% |
| 3. Large-Scale Cost and Capacity Optimization | 18% |
| 4. Security and Compliance Integration | 18% |
| 5. Migration and Lifecycle | 15% |
| 6. Enterprise Quality Governance | 12% |

**Domain 1: Organizational Requirements and Adoption Strategy**

- Knowledge: Different roles of enterprise chat apps (ChatGPT Enterprise, Claude Enterprise, Gemini Enterprise) and API development; advantages and disadvantages of multi-vendor operations.
- Skills: Distinguish departmental needs addressable through enterprise-app configuration from those requiring custom development.

**Domain 2: Enterprise Platform Architecture**

- Knowledge: AI gateways, multi-model routing, shared retrieval, enforcing document permissions in search results, centralized connector/MCP server management.
- Skills: Design shared knowledge bases used by multiple business units without exposing one unit's documents to another.

**Domain 3: Large-Scale Cost and Capacity Optimization**

- Knowledge: Provisioned Throughput, Priority/Flex tiers, batches, large-scale caching, departmental usage attribution.
- Skills: Combine billing options for workloads mixing steady traffic and spikes.

**Domain 4: Security and Compliance Integration**

- Knowledge: Zero-retention options, regional processing, admin controls, audit logs, prompt/response filtering such as Model Armor, and enterprise-app security settings.
- Skills: Select configurations balancing compliance and operational simplicity across countries with different regulations.

**Domain 5: Migration and Lifecycle**

- Knowledge: Model deprecation policies, official migration guides, API-generation changes (such as Responses migration and platform name/path changes), and prompt portability.
- Skills: Plan model replacement across dozens of services using evaluation gates and phased deployment.

**Domain 6: Enterprise Quality Governance**

- Knowledge: Shared organizational evaluation criteria, production quality monitoring, and risk categories in the three providers' safety frameworks.
- Skills: Unify differing team quality standards into common release criteria.
